Add MS 4107 keeps the instructions Peterborough actually received, signed by the Queen at the head and the foot. The heading is in clear: Instructions for Our Right Trusty and Right Welbeloved Cousin and Councillor Charles Earl of Peterborow and Monmouth. Given at Our Court at St James’s the Two and Twentieth day of February 1711/2 in the Tenth Year of Our Reign. The date is Old Style, so the year is 1712, and DECODE’s range 1711–1712 refers to this one letter. The same syllable 422 begins both abandon and abjuring . Before the print was found, four of these values (894 him , 466 he , 894.1098 himself , 981 your ) had already been guessed from the clear words around them. The code pads the text heavily with nulls. There are 414 groups for 232 printed words, and a single word can take four or five groups: his is written 328.333.388.467 once, and him 326.332.349.467.2269. Some words have more than one group ( Prince is 1076 or 2211; Rome is 1369 or 519.488). The numbers do not follow the alphabet (466 he , 609 his , 894 him , 981 your ), so this is not one of the printed one-part forms kept in SP 106/7. Two single groups have no word in the print: 91 after church of Rome and , and 261 in affairs 261 bring him . They are either nulls or small differences between the draft and the fair copy.

The text below is as printed by Parke, with his spelling modernised. The words in bold are the ones in code in the manuscript. We taking into our serious consideration the great endeavours that are used to pervert our good cousin , the Electoral Prince of Saxony , to the superstitious worship of the church of Rome , and the infinite prejudice and dishonour the Protestant interest would suffer if so considerable a Prince , in whose country the reformation first began , should abandon the principles of our most holy religion , think it a duty incumbent on us to prevent , as far as in us lies , so fatal a blow . For that end, we have taken the resolution of sending you to the said Prince, whom you are to join, if possible, before his arrival at Rome , yet in such a manner that your falling-in with him may appear merely accidental : but whether you meet him on the road, or find him at Rome , you shall take a proper opportunity to deliver our letter to him, accompanying it with expressions of our friendship and real concern for his prosperity . You shall endeavour to insinuate yourself into his good opinion , and, as occasion offers, urge the strongest arguments you can for keeping him steady to the Protestant religion . If you find your representations make any impression upon his mind , you shall then open to him the subject of your commission , and declare that we have dispatched you to him on purpose to let him know that we have still the same earnest desire of seeing him which we have so often expressed ; and that if he persists in those good resolutions he formerly had , to adhere firmly to the religion in which he was educated, he may depend upon a friendly and honourable reception in our Court , in case his inclination or the situation of his affairs bring him this way . If, upon discourse with him , you shall discover that he apprehends himself under a necessity of abjuring his religion , to avoid the dangers and difficulties he will otherwise be exposed to, and that he has an inclination to make his escape , you may concert with him the proper measures for rescuing him out of the hands he is in , and bringing him safe to our dominions, or those of any other Protestant Prince or State . If you should happen to be arrived at Turin when these our instructions are delivered to you, you shall acquaint the Duke of Savoy that, in compliance with your request, we have given you leave to see the city of Rome ; for you are by all means to prevent any suspicion of the true intent of your going thither . The nature of this service in which we now employ you is such, that we can neither enjoin you to correspond with either of our Secretaries of State , nor limit the time of your return ; we therefore leave it entirely to your discretion and prudence to come back to Turin when you shall judge your attendance on the Prince of no further use . The Prince was Frederick Augustus, son of Augustus the Strong and later Augustus III of Poland. Parke’s note explains that, expecting to marry a Catholic archduchess, the Prince “was about to set off for Rome, to abjure the Protestant religion”. The clerk put into code everything that named the Prince, the religion, or the mission and its cover story. The courtesies and the instructions about conduct stayed in clear.

Decrypting it with each of the 94 Rákóczi chancery keys on DECODE and scoring the output as Hungarian picked the syllabic key R609, which was applied unchanged. 97.6% of the groups decipher as sense: Muscovite and Polish envoys, the Tsar seeking peace with Charles XII, and the Swedes at Vilna. 231 · 27 · 221 · 219 · 80 · 77 · 10 · 1 · 86 · 125 · 77 Moszkva · és · lengyel · követ · e · k · j · ö · t · te · k — “Muscovite and Polish envoys came” 231 Mosqua · 270 Svéd · 285 Vajda · 252 Porta Jászvásár (Iaşi) → Ferenc Rákóczi II · Hungarian syllabic nomenclator · 8 March 1706 András Bay to Rákóczi, from the Moldavian court, 1706 Go to the full text ↓ MNL OL G15 Caps. D. Fasc. 81. 5 (DECODE R478), two pages, catalogued as a homophonic letter with no decryption and no key. The letter is one sheet written on both sides. Clear Hungarian passages alternate with runs of comma-separated numbers from 1 to 300 and two signs. It is dated at the foot Jászvásár 8. Martii and signed Bay András . The key is DECODE R609, a Rákóczi chancery key of 1703–1711 in the same fonds. Its letters have homophones (A 7/70, E 8/80, I 9/90, O 6/60, U 5/59), and it has two-digit consonant–vowel syllables (30 ba to 148 vu ), short words (27 és , 28 az , 13 hogy , 14 mért ) and a nomenclator from 149 to 293 (231 Mosqua, 221 Lengyel, 270 Svéd, 285 Vajda, 252 Porta, 236 Nagyságod). The nulls are 15–19, 200, 300, Ψ and +. The letter uses the nulls 16, 18, 19, 200, 300 and Ψ. An earlier issue of the same table, R561, scored second.

Valamint ez előtt negyed nappal küldött levelemben nyilván meg írtam,» Moszkva és lengyel követek jöttek ide; az lengyel vissza is ment, a moszkva még itt vagyon. Az mint expiscálhattam, olyat mondottak mind ketten: a moszkva békességre kéri a svédet, minden elvött várakat és ezen hadakozásban lött expensáit a svédnek megígérvén, «[ha oly] conditióval, hogy …» ellene a moszkva hadát declarálja-é a svéd «is» colligatióban «légyen». … Az moszkva követ «innét» Constantinápolyba «vagy» Erdélybe megyen, én nem tudhatni; mert csak maga beszéllett az vajdával, görögül. «…» Tegnapi napon az vajda tolmácsával conversatióban lévén, «… in discursu» Pekri uram általa olyat izent a vajdának, hogy csak Nagyságod a magyar nemzet dolgát complanálhassa a némettel, … minden szándéka Nagyságodnak a török ellen való hadakozás. «…» Az tolmácsot [… ?] tudván az barát az Portának szemének és fülének lenni, még nem mondotta; «nékem is» lelkemre kötötte, hogy ki ne adjam őtet. A svéd Vilnához szállott, mely Litvánia és Moszkva-Oroszország között vagyon. «… Jászvásár 8. Martii … Bay András.» In English. As I wrote four days ago, Muscovite and Polish envoys have come here; the Pole has gone back, the Muscovite is still here. As far as I could fish it out, both said that the Tsar is asking the Swede for peace, promising the Swede all the fortresses he has taken and his expenses in this war, on condition that the Swede declare [war?] against… Whether the Muscovite envoy goes on to Constantinople or to Transylvania I cannot tell, because he talked to the voivode alone, in Greek. Yesterday I talked with the voivode’s interpreter. Pekri had sent the voivode word through him that if only Your Highness can settle the Hungarian nation’s affairs with the Germans [the Emperor] …, Your Highness’s whole intention is war against the Turk. Knowing the friar to be the Porte’s eyes and ears, the interpreter has not yet told him, and he made me swear on my soul not to give him away. Valamint ez előtt negyed nappal küldött levelemben nyilván meg írtam,» Moszkva és lengyel követek jöttek ide; az lengyel vissza is ment, a moszkva még itt vagyon. Az mint expiscálhattam, olyat mondottak mind ketten: a moszkva békességre kéri a svédet, minden elvött várakat és ezen hadakozásban lött expensáit a svédnek megígérvén, «[ha oly] conditióval, hogy a ki[rály]» ellene a moszkva hadát declarálja-é a svéd «is, [ha nem]» colligatióban «légyen». Reményik(?), hogy szándékoznék; az moszkva követ «innét» Constantinápolyba «vagy» Erdélybe megyen, én nem tudhatni; mért csak maga beszéllett az vajdával, görögül. «…» Tegnapi napon az vajda tolmácsával conversatióban lévén, «… elő in discursu» Pekri uram általa olyat izent a vajdának, hogy csak Nagyságod a magyar nemzet dolgát complanálhassa a némettel, … minden szándéka Nagyságodnak a török ellen való hadakozás. «…» Az tolmácsot [? ha az … asseráltad-é ?] tudván az barát az Portának szemének és fülének lenni, még nem mondotta; «nékem is» lelkemre kötötte, hogy ki ne adjam őtet. A svéd Vilnához szállott, mely Litvánia és Moszkva-Oroszország között vagyon. «Továbbá is … Jászvásár 8. Martii … Bay András.» English gist: As written four days ago, Muscovite and Polish envoys have come here [to the Moldavian court]; the Pole has gone back, the Muscovite is still here. Both said the Tsar is asking the Swede for peace, promising him all the fortresses he has taken and his war expenses, on condition that [Charles XII] declare against... [text uncertain]; whether the Muscovite envoy goes on to Constantinople or Transylvania I cannot tell; he talked with the voivode alone, in Greek. Yesterday, in conversation with the voivode's interpreter: Pekri sent word to the voivode through him that if only Your Highness can settle the Hungarian nation's affairs with the Germans [the Emperor] ..., Your Highness's whole intention is war against the Turk. The interpreter, knowing the friar to be the Porte's eyes and ears, has not told him; he made me swear not to give him away. The Swede has moved to Vilna, between Lithuania and Muscovy. Philippe de Béthune, younger brother of Rosny (the future Sully), left for Rome with his instruction of 23 August 1601 (no. 2 of the volume) and served as ordinary ambassador until 1605. The letters of the King to him in fr. 3484 run from October 1601 to October 1602. They are the sent originals, signed Henry and countersigned de Neufville , that is Villeroy’s office, and the cipher is that office’s. Where the office in Rome deciphered a letter it wrote the decipherment in the margin, in a smaller hand, numbered 1, 2, 3 to the passages, or as a footnote keyed with a sign; the volume keeps those decipherments. Three letters have none. Bazeries ( Les chiffres secrets dévoilés , 1901, pp. 28–29) prints the “chiffre baillé à M. de Béthune” of 1599, given to Maximilien for his mission to England. Each letter has a figure (A = 3, B = 10, C = 8 …) and two or three arbitrary symbols; thirty names are figures with two dots ( Le Roy 4̈, Le Roy d’Espagne 2̈); some eighty common words are letters with a comma ( a, ayant … y, et, z, nous), with one dot (entre … mons) or with two dots (nostre … selon), each series alphabetical; the figures 2 to 11 with a comma are tout, tant, toutesfois … vivs ; a Δ doubles the preceding letter and y and $ cancel it. The 1601 cipher of the younger brother is the same office’s design two years on, with new values: f, = le, g, = la, x, = que, r, = par, q, = pour, d, = je in the comma series (the initials run l, l, q, p, p, j: alphabetical by groups, as in 1599); f: = au, s: = dit, x: = et, y: = ent in the two-dot series; t. = de, p. = ce with one dot; 61 = qui, 63 = re, 65 = si as syllable groups; 48 = Cardinal, 17 = Aldobrandin, 7 = le Roy d’Espagne as names; 68 = tout and 71 = tion are further syllable groups ( toutes = 68 ȥ g, affectionne ends 71 g ȥ). The letters: e = ȥ ‡ ε 0; a = 4 6 u; i = hooked m, v, a, 1; o = f + t; t = q 7; u/v = ꝑ, y, c; s = g, 2-shaped r, n; r = r ∂; l = h B S; m = x; g = plain m, hooked u; c = b e; p = o T; b = n; y = a. The sign φ is the doubling sign Bazeries describes in the 1599 key (“Δ doublera son prochain précédent”): somme is written s-o-m-φ-e, l’année l-a-n-φ-e-φ, Sillery has h-φ for ll , occasions o-c-φ, retrouve u-φ (u and v one letter), mienne mie-n-φ-e. The minute gives the enciphered passages word for word (differences: one word-sign where the minute has “de sorte”, “faites semblant” for the minute’s “taschez qu’il n’en soit rien dit”). In the King’s voice: after the Parlement of Paris had given judgment in the Este–Aldobrandini debt, he “fus bien aise d’avoir ce pretexte de gratifier led. Cardinal et luy tesmoigner ma bonne volonté … de sorte je luy fis payer des lors dix mil escuz par l’entremise du sieur de Sillery”; he has now ordered “qu’il face payer aud. Cardinal dedans les premiers quatre mois de l’année prochaine la somme de dix mil escuz par les mesmes mains … sans avoir esgard à l’arrest obtenu par lad. duchesse de Nemours, ny au besoing d’argent auquel je me retrouve. Car j’affectionne led. Cardinal et desire m’acquitter de lad. promesse que je luy ay faicte”; Béthune, after conferring with Cardinal d’Ossat, is to let Cardinal Aldobrandini know “de facon qu’il recoive et estime ceste grace comme elle merite”, to pretend “que vous n’aiez receu la presente”, and to be “le premier qui en avertira led. Cardinal Aldobrandin”. Pietro Aldobrandini, the Pope’s nephew, had made the Peace of Lyon in January 1601; in this letter the King pays for it and manages how the gift is announced. The full text is in the repository ( targets/bethune/reading_10nov.md ).

This letter was expected to be the harder of the two open ones: forty lines of cipher in blocks, the notice said, with no clear copy anywhere in the volume. The four leaves at full resolution show otherwise. The cipher is broken into eighty short runs set inside lines of ordinary clear French: the King’s secretary enciphered only the names, the sums and the sharpest judgements and left the grammar around them in clear. The clear text therefore carries most of the sense, and the content can be followed without decrypting the runs. All four pages are transcribed in targets/bethune/reading_22nov.md . No earlier transcription or decipherment of this letter was found in the volume, in Berger de Xivrey or in Colbert 17; Halphen’s edition (below) was not seen. It answers Béthune’s despatch of 29 October, received on the 18th, and is signed Henry and countersigned de Neufville . Its core is a rebuke, in clear, of two persons the cipher names only by code group: “Il me semble que [20] [S 12], qui sont douez de toute prudence, ont faict faulte de n’avoir rompu ce coup, car ilz l’eussent faict facilement s’ilz y eussent pensé et operé d’heure, ainsi qu’ilz devoient. Mais ilz se sont contentez de … meuz d’autres considerations …” On money and discipline the King will “donner ordre que la pension que j’ay accordée au s.r Camaiano sera bien payée”, all to “relever le party françois a Rome”; but Béthune is to give no “esperances ou [fermes] des promesses a d’autres” without express command, “afin de n’abuser personne ne moy le premier”, and to act always “après toutesfois en avoir conferé avec le Card.al d’Ossat”. He acknowledges the Pope’s “bon accueil … aux deux audiences quelle vous a données”; he will receive Maffeo Barberini (the future Urban VIII, then on his way to France) “le plus favorablement que je pourray po[ur] le respect de sa S.té”; on the Jesuits he refers back to an earlier letter and will await the Pope’s answer; and he complains of an agent “qui reside en Suisse, accompagné d’un certain Julio de la Torre y Travers[i]”, whom Cardinal Aldobrandini had already reprimanded. The third leaf ends in clear on the household news that dates the whole file: “J’attends en bonne devotion le retour du courrier que je vous ay envoié pour convier sa S.té au baptesme de mon filz, lequel se faict tres bien nourrir et se fortifie a veue d’oeil” . The son is the dauphin, born on 27 September. The letter is dated “Escrit a St Germain en Laye le xxij.e jour de 9bre 1601”, and a postscript, signed again, countermands part of what precedes it. The eighty ciphered runs are in targets/bethune/ct_22nov.txt . Decrypted with the key they give fragments only ( le cardinal aldobrandin , attenter a este toute , suisses , octobre , saincteté au ), the same ceiling the 9 November letter meets, for the same reason. Two values are confirmed by their clear frames, 73 = vostre and the pair 48 17 = Cardinal Aldobrandin . Fifteen groups remain open; three of them have frames that constrain them, and one, 72, has a proposal against it as well as for it (see below).

The corpus of known plaintext (the 10 November pair, the six glossed passages of 8 November, the footnote passage of 10 December, about 1,650 letters) was aligned by an EM procedure in which each symbol may stand for zero to twelve letters under a proper prior over strings, seeded with the values fixed by hand and allowing nulls only on the signs Bazeries’ design uses for them. The resulting P(letter | symbol) feeds the decoders. A second pass re-transcribed the leaf symbol by symbol at four times magnification, fixed the doubling sign, the syllable groups, ꝑ = u/v and a dozen letters on words of the minute, and raised the decryption to about six words in ten: …sera la promotion au cardinalat … Alexandre … ensemble ce que vous aurez … jamais il m’avoit dit … propos de rechercher le cardinal … de vous dire la res[olution] … de telles pratiques … des advis desdits car[dinaux] . A third pass added a bigram language model built from Xivrey’s 1.43 million words, which brought in sur le revenu de Naples , le nunce resident , les cardinaux … enclins a la [26] and aux prudens advis desdits card[inaux] . The letter concerns the Spanish pressure over Don Alexandre’s cardinalate and the cardinals’ advice; its clear opening had suggested military news. The third pass also gave a way of telling when to stop. An oracle bound lets every transcribed symbol emit any value in its model’s support and asks how many of the true letters it could then possibly produce. On the known-plaintext blocks that ceiling is 71.0 %, while the decoder scores 74.5 %: it is already above its own emission bound, getting a few letters right by accident. Further work on the search or the language model cannot help, because roughly 29 % of the true letters cannot be produced by the glyphs as transcribed. Ten things tried against that bound, all measured; none raised it. Widening each symbol’s emissions to those of its visually confusable partners raises the ceiling to 80.6 % but lowers the real decode from 74.5 % to 71.9 %: more ambiguity than the language model can resolve. Three segmentation architectures. Connected components give 1.13–1.38 components per glyph and both over- and under-cut. A forced alignment that never cuts (a dynamic program giving each token of a known sequence a variable-width slice, with templates re-estimated from the alignment) collapses to the average glyph from a uniform start. Restricting the cuts to component boundaries with a per-class width model leaves the program no freedom to recover where the components are wrong. More resolution. The second pass worked from Gallica’s 2,000-pixel image; the 3,926-pixel original gives about 30 % more linear resolution, and the glyphs are visibly crisper. It does not settle them. Letting the language model re-split the figures. The re-transcription located the disagreement in the figure runs rather than the letters, because the cipher writes figures without separators and one- and two-figure groups coexist, so “6165” can be divided as 61|65, 6|1|65 or 61|6|5. Offering every legal split to the decoder scores 70.8 %, and turns partant into “par [70] le roy d’Espaigne [2]”. Two independent transcriptions, combined. This is the one widening that helps. A block of 102 letters of known plaintext was transcribed again from scratch off the full-resolution leaf without consulting the first transcription. Transcription A (the second pass) scores 75.5 %, transcription B (the third) 57.8 %; they agree on 50 of 72 aligned positions, and their union reaches 78.4 %, nearly three points more. The second transcription is worse than the first, despite the extra resolution. Two careful transcriptions of the same ink agree on 69 % of its tokens. This hand does not carry enough information at roughly 450 dpi to fix its glyphs, which is what the 71 % bound says in another form. The confusions lie within the glyphs. In conduitte , whose decryption is verified against the minute, the same m-shaped glyph stands for d in one position and i in the next, the two differing only by a hook. The three families recorded earlier (an open-tailed and a looped g for n and s, three m -shapes for g, d, f, r against the 2-shaped r for r and s) are real, and no magnification separates them. The note in the repository that called the remainder “a day’s work, mechanical” has been corrected there, with the numbers; the two-digit names were not the obstacle.

The groups that carry the substance of both open letters (2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 20, 28, 31, 44, 66, 67, 69, 72, 80) occur only where there is no decipherment. Three have clear frames that constrain them: S 12 and 20 are the two persons “douez de toute prudence”; 28 is a place, from “ce[luy] m’a escrit de [28]”; 44 follows “et par consequent”. One has a proposal, recorded here the way this project records unconfirmed things. 72 = vous : the collocation “x , 72” ( que followed by 72) occurs four times across ff. 46r, 46v, 47r and 33; 72 opens a line three times; and on f. 53r, whose marginal decipherment is verbatim rather than a paraphrase, the gloss reads “…je ne suis pas d’auis que vous pressiez sa Sain.té…” exactly where the cipher runs x , 72 , T 63 , r S Z , which with the established T = p, 63 = re, r = s, Z = e gives que · vous · p-re-s-s-e . Against it: the block on f. 49v ends … 63 72 while its footnote gloss ends “il sera meilleur de differer a luy en parler”, where a final vous is hard to place. Either the ciphered block runs on past the passage the footnote glosses, or 72 is something else. It stays unconfirmed , and is used in no decryption on this page. The glossed leaves can settle them. At full resolution ff. 53r and 56r are tractable: their decipherments are verbatim, and whole clear phrases sit inside the ciphered blocks (“discours d’aultruy. Il fault” on f. 53r, “Mais je ne croy pas quil le face” and “si ce n’est pour” on f. 56r), each also in the gloss, in the gloss’s own order. These give fixed anchors for an alignment. f. 53r contains 66 and 72; f. 56r’s margins name the King of Spain and Archduke Albert in clear. Neither block is transcribed.
bethune.html#finish

The clear text of both open letters should exist in a copy register, and the search found the likely volume. BnF, Cinq cents de Colbert 346 is “Copies des despesches concernans l’ambassade de Messire Philippe de Bethune, conseiller du Roy en son Conseil d’Estat, à Rome, en 1601-[1605]”, whose first volume runs 23 August 1601 to 22 November 1602 and holds letters of Henri IV, Marie de Médicis, Villeroy and Béthune. That range covers both the 9 and the 22 November letters, and a copy register of this kind is made from the minutes, that is, in clear, which is how the 10 November letter could be deciphered here. It is not digitised: Gallica’s SRU returns no record for it. Consulting it in the Salle des manuscrits, or ordering reproductions, is the next step for this target. Separately, Eugène Halphen edited Lettres inédites du roi Henri IV à monsieur de Béthune, ambassadeur de France à Rome, du 18 octobre au 24 décembre 1601 , an edition covering precisely this stretch. It is in the HathiTrust catalogue (record 100644113) and not in Gallica, the Internet Archive or Open Library. Whether Halphen printed the ciphered passages in clear (which would have required the minutes) decides whether these letters count as already in print, as fr. 3077/3078 did for Du Bellay. Checked and excluded as sources of a clear text: Berger de Xivrey’s Recueil , vols. I–V, which prints a Béthune letter of 10 October 1601 but nothing for November; Mélanges de Colbert 17, whose first part is still running instructions at p. 179 and whose second is 1602–05; and BnF fr. 3677 and 3678, the “Registre des lettres que monseigneur de Bethune a escrites en France durant son ambassade de Rome”, which belong to the second embassy of 1624–30.

reading_10nov.md # Henri IV to Béthune, Paris, 10 November 1601 (BnF fr. 3484 f. 34) — the enciphered passages, read The sent original (f. 34r–v, signed Henry, countersigned de Neufville) puts four passages in cipher. The minute of the same letter, "Du Xe 9bre 1601" (f. 36r–v, item 9 of the notice, "copie du n° précédent"), is entirely in clear and gives their text; the cipher aligns with it symbol for symbol under the key in `key.tsv` (the EM alignment in `corpus.txt`, entries A, B1–B4, C, V1, V3). Spelling as in the minute; the clear parts of the sent letter in roman, the enciphered passages in *italics*; [ ] where the sent text differs from the minute or is uncertain. > Mons. de Bethune, Apres la prise de … [the Este–Aldobrandini debt and the Parlement's judgment] … contradictoirement > donné du parlement de ceste ville, *mais je fus bien aise d'avoir ce pretexte de gratifier led. Cardinal et luy > tesmoigner ma bonne volonté, et qu'il l'eust aussi de recevoir ma gratification, de sorte [que] je luy fis payer des > lors dix mil escuz par l'entremise du sieur de Sillery.* Ainsy que vous dira le Cardinal d'Ossat qui en a eu > cognoissance. … Pourquoy j'ay *advisé de gratifier led. Cardinal pour luy faire cognoistre en la prosperité* en > laquelle je me retrouve par la grace de Dieu *que je veux* aussy *bien recognoistre les plaisirs qu'il m'a faictz que > j'ay recherché son amitié en mes necessitez. Partant j'ay commandé à [Sillery's brother] qu'il face payer aud. > Cardinal dedans les premiers quatre mois de l'année prochaine la somme de dix mil escuz par les mesmes mains que il a > touché les premiers,* sans avoir esgard *à l'arrest obtenu par lad. duchesse de Nemours, ny au besoing d'argent auquel > je me retrouve. Car j'affectionne led. Cardinal et desire m'acquitter de lad. promesse que je luy ay faicte, et en > toutes occasions luy tesmoigner ma bonne volonté.* Au moien de quoy apres en avoir conferé aud. Card. d'Ossat vous > ferez savoir aud. Card. Aldobrandin ce que dessus *de facon qu'il recoive et estime ceste grace comme elle merite > [car autrement] le fault [seroit …]* Ainsy que le desire led. Aldobrandin pour les raisons que vous apprendrez dud. > Card. d'Ossat. Faites *doncques valoir ceste mienne bonne volonté par vostre bonne conduitte et [faites semblant]* > que vous n'aiez receu la presente affin que vous soiez *le premier qui en avertira led. Cardinal Aldobrandin.* Je > prie dieu qu'il vous ait Mons. de Bethune en sa saincte garde. De Paris ce Xe jour de Novembre 1601. Henry. What it says: after the Parlement of Paris had decided the Este–Aldobrandini debt (the sums the Este dukes owed the Aldobrandini), the King seized the occasion to gratify Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, the Pope's nephew: 10,000 écus paid at once through Sillery, 10,000 more promised for the first four months of 1602 by the same channel, regardless of the arrêt the Duchess of Nemours had obtained and of the King's own want of money, "car j'affectionne led. Cardinal". Béthune is to arrange with Cardinal d'Ossat how Aldobrandini is told, to seem not to have received this letter, and to be the first to announce it. Cardinal Aldobrandini had negotiated the Peace of Lyon in January 1601; this is the King's payment for it. Checks: the sent text and the minute agree in every aligned word except "de sorte" (cipher has one symbol, a,, where the minute has two words), "à mon frere" for Sillery's brother (minute: "a [Sillery?] frere"), and "faites semblant" (minute: "taschez qu'il n'en soit rien dit"). Unverified: the code groups 3, 7, 8, 64, 70, 71, 73 inside these passages are assigned by the alignment only. The text of the cipher passages rests on the clear minute of the same letter (f. 36r-v), aligned symbol for symbol with the cipher. --> # Henri IV to Béthune, Paris, 10 November 1601 (BnF fr. 3484 f. 34): English translation Monsieur de Béthune, after the taking of … [the Este–Aldobrandini debt and the Parlement's judgment] … given after hearing both parties by the Parlement of this city, *but I was very glad to have this pretext to gratify the said Cardinal and show him my goodwill, and that he too should have it for receiving my gratification, so [that] I had ten thousand écus paid to him at once through the agency of the Sieur de Sillery.* As the Cardinal d'Ossat, who knew of it, will tell you. … Wherefore I have *decided to gratify the said Cardinal, to let him know in the prosperity* in which I now find myself by the grace of God *that I mean* also *to acknowledge the kindnesses he has done me just as I sought his friendship in my necessities. Therefore I have ordered [Sillery's brother] to have the sum of ten thousand écus paid to the said Cardinal within the first four months of next year, by the same hands through which he received the first,* without regard *to the decree obtained by the said Duchess of Nemours, nor to the want of money in which I find myself. For I have affection for the said Cardinal, and wish to discharge the promise I made him, and on every occasion to show him my goodwill.* By means of which, after conferring about it with the said Cardinal d'Ossat, you will let the said Cardinal Aldobrandini know the above, *in such a way that he receives and values this favour as it deserves, [for otherwise] it would be necessary [ … ]* As the said Aldobrandini wishes, for the reasons you will learn from the said Cardinal d'Ossat. *So make the most of this goodwill of mine by your good conduct, and [pretend]* that you have not received the present letter, so that you may be *the first to inform the said Cardinal Aldobrandini of it.* I pray God, Monsieur de Béthune, to keep you in His holy care. From Paris, this 10th day of November 1601. Clear French with runs of figures. Where British Library, Add MS 32305 ff. 6–7, catalogued as “unidentified cipher keys”; DECODE R2964 and R2965. The volume is a codebreaker’s working file of intercepts. The cipher A two-part code of three-figure groups, about 900 entries. The 7 February letter has 354 groups, 191 distinct, 116 of them seen once. How it was tried The first letter was transcribed with the decipherer’s glosses. The glosses are not in alphabetical order, so the code is two-part and its order says nothing about the other values. Still open Everything but the dozen glossed values. A key, a clear copy or many more letters in the code would be needed. Catalogue item 78 listed six DECODE records of this volume under one unknown sender in Paris. The images show a working file of unrelated intercepts. This page is the Paris 1719 code. The letters to Mr Carré in Pall Mall, 1742–45 (R2968, R2970, R2972), are in a different code: Letters to Mr Carré, 1742–45 (a different cipher, with its own page). R2963 and R2974, and the other records around them, were deciphered at the time in their own ciphers.

R2964, f. 6r: “J’avois été deja informé par” and the code, with the decipherer’s que (184), qu’il (652) and vous (243) above. Image: British Library, Add MS 32305 f. 6r, via DECODE R2964. The writer reports Lord Stair’s formal entry into Paris and his audience with the King, and tells his correspondent that he will stay in England “jusqu’au retour de S. M. Brit.” The clear text uses a family cover (“vos Parens”, “votre Cousin”, “le caractère des esprits de votre Famille”), and the second letter opens on the coming war with Spain and Cardinal Alberoni. The persons are figures marked with a cross: 27, 258, 285, 611. The decipherer glossed 36 = re, 88 = pas, 95 = le, 184 = que, 243 = vous, 347 = a, 531 = pour, 652 = qu’il and 786 = s, the same values in both letters. That is 33 of the 354 groups of the first letter. In a one-part code, where values run in alphabetical order, these would bracket the rest. Here re (36) comes before pas (88), le (95) and que (184), and a comes at 347, so the code is two-part and its order says nothing. The Carré letters of 1742–45 in the same volume are in another two-part code, of about 800 entries. With about 700 groups in the two letters for a code of some 900 entries, most values occur once, and the decipherer glossed no more than the recurring values.

The decipherer of the time wrote the plaintext letter by letter over every line (“…que l’on ignore pas les dangers auxquels notre position nous expose… les insinuations de Mr de Guydickens…”). R2979 (f. 34), “Hanau to Fer., Hague 9 Aout 1753”, is the decipherer’s own working copy of a letter in a 4-figure syllable and word code. The clear syllables are written out and the groups he decoded are glossed (1688 = si , 1560 = roi , 3227 = Devonshire). The rest are left as figures, and the sheet ends “Ici on parle du mariage de 3245 avec 3263” beside a column of question marks. The first record was deciphered in full at the time, and the second in part. Item 79 has been removed from the catalogue.

Four cipher letters of the Branicki family archive in Warsaw, listed as unsolved: Hetman Branicki’s plan of a manifesto (22 March 1757), a field report from the Russian army, a fund of 146,000 francs to buy the Lithuanian dietines, and a bloody dietine at Brest. Prabal Gupta found a reciprocal alphabet of twelve pairs from the ciphertext of the first letter, and the same key reads the others; 97.5% of the cipher words read, 1398 only in part. b p n m b p l · e l · u c n m l f · r n o r l c f l … quoique · le · proiet · concerte … Białystok · reciprocal letter alphabet and a number code · 1756–57 · key found by a contributor Branicki to Potocki and three Lithuanian letters, 1756–57 Go to the full text ↓ Hetman Branicki’s plan of a manifesto, a field report from the Russian army, a fund of 146,000 francs for the Lithuanian dietines and a bloody dietine at Brest: four letters, one key. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (98% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Prabal Gupta (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (98% of the cipher) The letters Four cipher letters of the Branicki family archive: Hetman Jan Klemens Branicki to Antoni Potocki, palatine of Bełz, from Białystok on 22 March 1757 (the catalogue says May); a field report from the Russian army in July 1757; an insider’s report on the fund of the Lithuanian magnates to buy the dietines (1756); and an account of a bloody dietine at Brest, signed Boeven, of 11 September 1756. Where Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych (AGAD), Warsaw, Zbiór Anny z Potockich Ksawerowej Branickiej (zesp. 338), 1/338/0/1/446, 1398, 1399 and 1400 (catalogue 1578 and 1579). Not on DECODE. The cipher A reciprocal alphabet: twelve pairs of letters that swap (a stands for h and h for a, b for q, c for r …), with i and j, u and v merged, and a nomenclator of three-digit numbers for titles, names and places in alphabetical order, with number words and nulls. How it was deciphered Prabal Gupta found the alphabet from the ciphertext of letter 446 with a count-matching algorithm on French next-letter counts; the same key reads the other three letters with no change, and he built the number code from clear text beside the cipher and the alphabetical order. Checked here: the decryption follows from the transcription and the key, and a word-list test covers 53–59% of the letters against at most 27% for any of 300 shuffled keys. What it says Branicki plans a manifesto against the abuse an envoy makes of his mission; the Russian army under Apraxin stands at the frontier of Prussia; a congress at Iwie deposits 146,000 francs to buy the coming dietines, and the five shares add up; at Brest a rival party that spent 200,000 francs has its own deputies elected. Still open The rough second page of 1398, some number codes, and a human check of the transcriptions against the AGAD scans, which the project could not reach. Credit The key, transcriptions and readings are Prabal Gupta’s (issues #316 and #317; repository , CC BY 4.0). The scans were not seen here and are not reproduced.
branicki1757.html#the-letters

In 1756–57 the Seven Years’ War brought a Russian army to the frontier of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, whose magnates were divided into parties for and against the Czartoryski “Familia”. Jan Klemens Branicki was grand hetman of the Crown, and the catalogue calls him the head of the party against the Familia; the letters themselves speak of the dietines, the Tribunal and the money spent to win them. His family archive in Warsaw keeps letters in cipher that the archive’s cards mark as not deciphered. Letter 446 is one of his own, in French, with a clear opening and close around a paragraph in cipher. The three others are reports to a patron: 1398 from an agent with the Russian army, 1399 from a man close to the Lithuanian grand hetman Radziwłł, and 1400 from Nieśwież. How these men fit the parties is the contributor’s reading from a 1909 history, not checked here. Letter 446’s dateline gives 22 March 1757. The catalogue’s “May” was a misreading at low resolution.
branicki1757.html#the-key

The key swaps letters in pairs: a-h, b-q, c-r, d-s, e-l, f-t, g-z, i-m, k-x, n-o, p-u, w-y. The contributor’s count-matching algorithm found it on the cipher of letter 446 and returned it, on 1399 and 1400 taken alone, on 99.4% and 98.9% of tokens; applied unchanged, it reads 1398, 1399 and 1400 as French. The three-digit numbers are a table in alphabetical order (215 Castellan, 330 Excellence, 575 Palatin, 620 Prince, 625 Prusse, 655 Russie, 740 Tribunal), with number words at 805 to 824, so that 1400 dates itself in cipher: 824 811 823 818 810, “mil sept cent cinquante six”. Where the writer left a name in clear next to the cipher, the number was matched to it: “Mr le Palatin de Trok” in clear and “Mr le [575] de Trok” in cipher. Checks made here, with the scans out of reach: the decryption of 446 follows from the transcription and the key on every line; a list of about 140 common French words covers 0.53 to 0.59 of the decrypted letters of the four letters, against 0.27 at most for any of 300 shuffled keys; and the five shares of 1399, 53,000 + 25,000 + 50,000 + 10,000 + 8,000, add up to the 146,000 francs the letter states. A French language model could not be built from this environment, so the project’s n-gram validation is not applicable.
branicki1757.html#the-reading

Letter 446 reads at 96.7% (12 holes in 369 cipher words), 1399 at 98.3% and 1400 at 99.4%; 1398 reads at 95.5%, but its second page has a rough transcription and a reading that repairs garbled stretches by sense, so it is the one part only partly deciphered. Over the four letters 97.5% of the cipher words are deciphered. In English, Branicki writes: “Although the plan agreed at Warsaw meets obstacles from our friends, I do not at all believe that we should lose sight of it … the most pressing matter is the abuse that Mr the Stolnik of Lithuania makes of his mission … I believe there is no time to lose for the publication of the manifesto that I want to make together with you and your whole house.” The contributor reads the envoy as Stanisław Poniatowski, later king, who held that title and was in St Petersburg; that identification, like his reading of Boeven as the hetman’s secretary on the French payment list, rests on one printed book that was not opened here. The Spanish, French and English texts are under Full texts.

À Bialystok, ce 22 mars 1757. ## En clair Monseigneur, J'ai reçu la lettre que Votre Excellence m'a fait l'honneur de m'écrire le 6 de ce mois, et je ne perds pas un moment pour y faire réponse. ## En chiffre Quoique le projet concerté à Varsovie rencontre des obstacles de la part de nos amis, je ne crois nullement que nous devions le perdre de vue. Je prévois même des [?événements] qui en rendront l'exécution indispensable. Mais l'objet le plus pressant qui doit nous occuper dans ce moment est l'abus que fait Mr le [?Stolnik] [de] Lithuanie de sa mission. La prévoyance et les lumières de votre Excellence me sont trop connues pour m'étendre avec elle sur les suites malheureuses que cet envoy entraînera aprez lui, dont la moindre est le mépris général dans lequel la République va tomber au dehors, quand on verra que personne d'entre nous ne se lève contre une violation si ouverte des loix fondamentales de l'état. N'est-il pas d'ailleurs très vraisemblable que la Russie fera valoir ce prétexte pour exiger de la [?Pologne] un dédommagement d'une partie des fraix de la guerre à laquelle ce prétendu ministre l'a invitée de la part du [?Roi] ? Je crois donc, Monseigneur, qu'il n'y a pas de tems à perdre pour la publication du manifeste que je veux faire de concert avec vous et avec toute votre maison. J'en ai déjà prévenu Mr le Palatin [?de Kiovie] [?et le Czesnik] ; ce dernier est très résolu de se joindre à moi dans une affaire si intéressante pour la patrie, et je me flatte que d'autres bons patriotes se feront un devoir de suivre notre exemple. J'en ai même des assurances très positives de quelques palatinats. Je suis donc convenu avec Mr le Palatin [?de Kiovie] [480] et avec [?le Czesnik] de la couronne de m'aboucher avec eux vers la fin du mois prochain, les priant de vouloir se rendre ici pour ce tems-là, ou bien m'indiquer un endroit où je puisse aller les joindre. Je prie votre Excellence de ne pas nous refuser sa présence dans une [?occasion] de cette importance, où nous pourrons en même tems nous arranger sur le parti à prendre suivant les conjonctures. [367] Comme il n'y a encore rien de décidé sur la route que prendront les troupes russiennes, je réglerai ma résolution là-dessus par rapport au séjour que je pourrai choisir pour m'y fixer, en attendant le retour de la [?paix]. ## En clair J'ignore en effet quelles peuvent être les vues de Mr le Staroste de Kaniow et de Madame la Castellane de Kamien, qui le guide. Je sais que j'ai porté dans cette affaire ma complaisance plus loin qu'elle ne devait aller, dont j'ai grand sujet de me repentir, parce que je n'en ai aucune reconnaissance. Mr Delachinal ne m'a jamais prié de lui faire grâce des arrêts. C'est sur les instances de Mr le Palatin de Kiovie et de Mr le Czesnik de la Couronne que je me suis relâché sur cette partie du décret. D'ailleurs cet officier vient de quitter le service de la République, ce qu'il n'aurait pas fait s'il ne se fût trouvé impliqué dans un procès si fâcheux. Le Major Auspitz garde les arrêts depuis plus de trois mois. Les discours que Madame la Castellane a tenus sur mon compte et les démarches qui se font en conséquence me dispensent de tous les ménagements ultérieurs. Je ne mande aucune nouvelle à Votre Excellence, sachant que ses autres correspondants ne les lui laissent point ignorer. En demandant la continuation de son amitié, je lui offre toute l'étendue de la mienne et les assurances de l'attachement respectueux avec lequel j'ai l'honneur d'être, Monseigneur, de Votre Excellence le très humble et très obéissant serviteur, Comte Branicki. Białystok, 22 March 1757. ## In clear Monseigneur, I have received the letter that Your Excellency did me the honour of writing to me on the 6th of this month, and I do not lose a moment in replying. ## In cipher Although the plan agreed at Warsaw meets obstacles from our friends, I do not at all believe that we should lose sight of it. I even foresee [?events] that will make carrying it out indispensable. But the most pressing matter that must occupy us at this moment is the abuse that Mr the [?Stolnik] of Lithuania is making of his mission. The foresight and insight of Your Excellency are too well known to me for me to dwell on the unhappy consequences this sending will bring after it, the least of which is the general contempt into which the Republic will fall abroad, when people see that no one among us rises against so open a violation of the fundamental laws of the state. Is it not, besides, very likely that Russia will use this pretext to demand from [?Poland] compensation for part of the costs of the war, to which this so-called minister invited her on behalf of the [?King]? So I believe, my lord, that there is no time to lose in publishing the manifesto that I want to make together with you and with your whole house. I have already told Mr the Palatine [?of Kiev] [?and the Czesnik]; the latter is firmly resolved to join me in an affair so important for the fatherland, and I flatter myself that other good patriots will make it their duty to follow our example. I even have very positive assurances of this from some palatinates. So I have agreed with Mr the Palatine [?of Kiev] [480] and with [?the Czesnik] of the Crown to confer with them toward the end of next month, asking them to come here at that time, or else to name a place where I can go and join them. I beg Your Excellency not to refuse us your presence at an [?occasion] of this importance, where we can at the same time agree on the course to take according to events. [367] As nothing is yet decided about the route that the Russian troops will take, I shall settle my decision on that, as to the stay I may choose in order to fix myself there, while awaiting the return of [?peace]. ## In clear I do not indeed know what the aims may be of Mr the Staroste of Kaniów and of Madame the Castellane of Kamieniec, who guides him. I know that in this affair I carried my indulgence further than it should have gone, and I have good reason to repent of it, because I get no gratitude for it. Mr Delachinal never asked me to spare him the arrest. It was at the urging of Mr the Palatine of Kiev and Mr the Czesnik of the Crown that I relaxed this part of the decree. Besides, this officer has just left the service of the Republic, which he would not have done if he had not found himself caught in so vexing a lawsuit. Major Auspitz has been under arrest for more than three months. The remarks that Madame the Castellane has made about me, and the steps being taken as a result, release me from all further consideration. I send Your Excellency no news, knowing that your other correspondents keep you informed. Asking for the continuation of your friendship, I offer you the full extent of mine, and the assurances of the respectful attachment with which I have the honour to be, Monseigneur, Your Excellency's very humble and very obedient servant, Count Branicki. The news from this place is that Count Apraxin is still at his headquarters at [?Ludwinow], seven leagues from the frontier of Prussia, and it is believed he will not enter Prussia so quickly. The shortage here is extraordinary, especially of [?flour], and even all the pastures around where the army passed, for three leagues, are completely ruined by a great number of horses. Great provisions are carried continually from the general magazines of Kowno, of [?Skorul] and of Wilkomierz to the Russian army. This transport is devastating the country, taking horses and men without pay to carry its provisions. Men are [?beaten], and it is very hard to get satisfaction for the damage done by the Cossacks and Kalmyks. ## Page 2, rough At the moment I write this letter, the news has come that Count Apraxin is to come to [?Wierzbolowy], to camp there, half a league from the limits of Prussia. The deputies of the towns of Prussia have come to Field Marshal Apraxin, submitting to him and imploring his mercy and military discipline. The towns are called [?Gumbin], [?Stolupiany], [?...]. [?...] for the town of Memel. Yet nothing is said except that Count Apraxin ordered the contributions and provisions, and he has even obliged Mr the Castellan and Mr the Marshal of Kowno to gather all kinds of provisions after the harvest, of which [?...] consequence. It is said that another Russian army, to reinforce this one, which consists of only sixty thousand men, is to come here, or that the present army, when the treaties are concluded, will come here for winter quarters. But it is to be feared that then we will see what [?formation] of our state. The officers of Prussia have talked with trusted persons both of the extraordinary [?suite] and of the succession to the throne [?...]. But on this point confirmation is needed, because only the ladies have said it. It is said that the Stolnik of [496] will marry the only daughter and very rich heiress of Field Marshal Apraxin. Of the army of the King of Prussia, I believe that His Excellency the Grand General of the Crown has enough reports that it is now under the town of [?Pillau] [?...]. The fortifications have been increased. Rumour says that the Prussians have mixed poison into the flour and the bread, to poison the Russians. [?...] of the King their master not to resist the Russians [?...]. I have also heard that if this [580] has come not to speak ill of the King of Prussia [?...]. I also beg you to prostrate me at the feet of His Excellency the Grand General as my only protector, and I am until the last breath of my life, Sir, your most faithful client Matusewic. I would very gladly have answered at once, if time had allowed it in any way, but I was still travelling when the post went out, and we were hardly left the time required, so I could not do as I wished. I have however made up for this by having my master do what I would have done myself, if time had allowed: I got him to send you a copy of the letter from Mr [195], dated the 30th of last month, which was not answered by this post. When it is, I will not fail to have a copy sent to you. If the reply holds anything of interest, I will also be very exact in telling you whatever deserves it, so far as my reports do not go against what I owe to God, my master, my conscience and my honour. We left Grodno on the 4th of this month and arrived on the 6th at Zdzięcioł, at the home of the Dowager Princess Palatine of Nowogród, a worthy daughter of our province, who hardly consoled us on the sad state of our present affairs. There we only planned to gather our friends on the twelfth of this month at Iwie, at the home of Mr the [385] of Lithuania, to decide what to do in so thorny a crisis. We spent only the night at Zdzięcioł, and arrived the next day at Korelicze, on our own lands. As soon as they knew we were there, the unfortunates came to find us, among them the Abramowicz gentlemen, all three, the two Bohusz and the Ciechanowiecki gentlemen, led by Mr the Prince [480] and the Strasznik of Lithuania. The pitiful looks and gestures of these wretches seemed to reproach us for our lack of firmness. We sent them back to the congress of Iwie, where they went that same day. We left Korelicz on the 10th before noon, and came to sleep at Sielup at the home of the Palatine of Trok, whom we also persuaded to go to the congress of Iwie, where we arrived on the evening of the 11th. There we found the Abramowicz, Bohusz and Ciechanowiecki families. The next day, the twelfth, there arrived Mr the Palatine of Trok with Mr the Strasznik of Lithuania, his son; Madame the Princess Palatine, dowager of Nowogród, with Mr the Prince [841] of Lithuania, her son; and Mr the Prince, Grand Ensign of this Grand Duchy. Since arriving, these gentlemen have already held several conferences, both at the home of Mr the [386] and at the Bernardines' of Iwie. So far I do not know the result, but it will surely reach me, and I will not fail to inform you. By this post I am setting up a new correspondence at Mitau, to be told exactly what is happening in Russia, and especially on the frontiers of [?Livonia] and [?Courland]. I will take care to let you know in time, so that you can pass it on where we agreed. But, Sir, subject to your better judgment, when I discover some [?event] of importance whose nature absolutely requires that it be known quickly, would it not be better, to avoid all delay, for me to go directly to the minister of [?France]? For I will find the means to write to him and to receive his orders without arousing the least suspicion in anyone. It is not that I wish, God forbid, to hide my discoveries from you, and I will always inform you of them with the utmost exactness. It is to cut short such circumstances where the case may require it. Please tell me frankly what you think. Just before our departure from Iwie, I learned the result of the conferences, and I do not fail to send it to you in this letter too. I do not believe I betray my master by letting you know, since I see that he has no secrets from his Excellency the Grand General of the Crown, and he may tell him the result himself. So it was agreed to deposit at Koydanow, with Mr the General Major [?Trabiwski], the sum of one hundred and forty-six thousand francs, to be shared out across all the palatinates and districts of Lithuania, to secure in our favour the success of the coming dietines, both for electing the deputies to the Diet and the deputies to the Tribunal of 1757. From this general sum, six thousand francs have already been drawn for Mr Zabiello, territorial marshal of Kowno, and eight thousand for Mr de Tiezenaus, palatinate ensign of Wilna. Five lords have undertaken to provide their shares by the 1st of next August, to make up this sum, namely: - the Prince Grand General, fifty-three thousand; - Mr the [385] of Lithuania, twenty-five thousand; - the Prince Grand Ensign, fifty thousand; - Mr Pociei, Strasznik of Lithuania, ten thousand; - and Mr Sottohub, General of Artillery, eight thousand. Il y eut cette fois à Brest de Lithuanie, pour l'élection des nonces à la Diète générale, une diétine des plus tumultueuses. Tout y respiroit que rage, fureur et carnage. Frère contre frère, parent contre parent s'y déchaînoit avec la dernière inhumanité. Mr le comte Sapieha Palatin s'y étoit trouvé pour maintenir le bon ordre et tâcher d'amener les choses au paisible choix de nonces dans ce palatinat, qui puissent entrer dans nos vues. Mais hélas, ce seigneur, dont les remontrances n'ont pu faire la moindre impression sur la noblesse furieuse, est heureux d'être échappé de ses mains sain et sauf. Tous, excepté un fort petit nombre, étoient du parti contraire, qui a élu arbitrairement pour nonces Mrs Oziemblowski et Suzin, lieutenant de Mr Sosnowski cassé par le décret connu, apparemment pour engager le Prince Grand Général à se relâcher en quelque façon de la rigueur de la sentence portée contre lui, quoique cette élection étant illégale ne pourra se soutenir. Une douzaine de gentilshommes, qui ne manqueront pas aussi de se rendre à Varsovie pour empêcher l'activité de ces nonces illégitimement élus, ayant protesté solennellement contre cet acte au grod de Bielsk en Podlachie. À la tête des mutins se trouvoit Mr [?Buchowiecki], notaire territorial dudit palatinat, autrefois de nos amis, mais qui depuis nous a tourné casaque. Celui-ci à cette diétine a bien taillé de la besogne à Mr le Palatin. Ce turbulent prétend encore jusqu'à présent engager ce palatinat à une revue [385] de la noblesse, premier pas d'une confédération. Mais Mr Wereszczaka, enseigne de ce palatinat, soutenu de Mr le Palatin, s'y oppose fortement. Tout ce remue-ménage provient de la libéralité du parti contraire, qui a répandu deux cent mille francs dans tous les palatinats et districts de Lithuanie. C'est pourquoi Mr le Palatin, prévoyant que la somme que nous étions sur le point de faire compter à ce palatinat n'effectueroit rien sur la noblesse déjà gagnée depuis longtemps par nos adversaires, a jugé à propos de ne la point hasarder inutilement. Je suis, Monsieur, votre très humble, très obéissant serviteur Boeven. P. S. À Nowogrod il fut impossible d'engager la noblesse d'insérer la réhabilitation du Sr Abramowicz dans l'instruction des nonces, la plupart, qui a des procès au Tribunal, appréhendant que [?la Famille] ne lui fasse payer bien cher une telle démarche. Mr Oziemblowski, un des nonces illégitimement élus à Brest de Lithuanie, towarzysz de Mr le Palatin, a quitté le service militaire. Nieśwież, 11 September 1756 Sir, Every day we hear here very tragic news of the dietines of our Lithuania. Whichever way one turns, one meets only the corpses of gentlemen massacred at these riotous assemblies, which are carried to the courts and to the Tribunal to be presented there: the deadly result of this hatred that is tearing apart the Republic. This time at Brest of Lithuania, for electing the deputies to the general Diet, there was a dietine of the most riotous kind. Everything there breathed only rage, fury and carnage. Brother against brother, kin against kin, were let loose with the utmost inhumanity. Count Sapieha, the Palatine, was there to keep good order, and to try to bring about a peaceful choice of deputies in this palatinate who could serve our aims. But alas, this lord, whose protests made not the least impression on the furious nobles, is lucky to have escaped their hands safe and sound. All of them, except a very small number, were of the opposite party, which arbitrarily elected as deputies Messrs Oziemblowski and Suzin, the lieutenant of Mr Sosnowski, who was struck down by the known decree. Apparently this was to get the Prince Grand General to relax somewhat the severity of the sentence passed against him, although this election, being illegal, will not hold. A dozen gentlemen, who will not fail to go to Warsaw as well to block the work of these illegally elected deputies, have solemnly protested against this act at the court of Bielsk in Podlachia. At the head of the mutineers was Mr [?Buchowiecki], territorial notary of that palatinate, once one of our friends, but who has since turned his coat. At this dietine he made plenty of work for Mr the Palatine. This troublemaker still claims he will bring this palatinate to a review [385] of the nobles, the first step toward a confederation. But Mr Wereszczaka, ensign of this palatinate, backed by Mr the Palatine, strongly opposes it. All this uproar comes from the generosity of the opposite party, which has scattered two hundred thousand francs across all the palatinates and districts of Lithuania. So Mr the Palatine, foreseeing that the sum we were about to pay out to this palatinate would achieve nothing with nobles long since won over by our adversaries, judged it best not to risk it for nothing. I am, Sir, your very humble and very obedient servant Boeven. P.S. At Nowogród it proved impossible to get the nobles to include the rehabilitation of Sieur Abramowicz in the deputies' instructions. Most of them, who have lawsuits before the Tribunal, fear that [?the Familia] would make them pay dearly for such a step. Mr Oziemblowski, one of the deputies illegally elected at Brest of Lithuania, a towarzysz of Mr the Palatine, has left military service. Key: key.tsv

Comenius, at Leszno during the Swedish invasion of Poland, ended his report of 4 August 1655 to Rákóczi’s councillor with one ciphered sentence. Szilágyi printed its decipherment in 1890 and Patera in 1892; the key rebuilt from it is the reciprocal table of Rákóczi’s envoys that Szilágyi had printed in 1874, with one letter in conflict. A second cipher passage, of 24 May 1655, does not decipher with that table or as a simple substitution of Latin. Cyhyqbma cgzbbttg, et CmCasda 69 655m poloniam periisse, et papatum in illa a = m · b = i · c = p · t = s Leszno → Andreas Klobusiczky · reciprocal letter substitution · 24 May and 4 Aug 1655 · existing decipherment, partial Comenius to Andreas Klobusiczky, 1655 from Jan Amos Comenius Go to the full text ↓ Two cipher passages in Comenius’s reports to Rákóczi’s councillor: the August sentence was deciphered in print in 1890 and its key is the Rákóczi court table; the May passage does not yield to it. Two letters carry a cipher passage: 24 May (unsigned) and 4 August (unsigned, the sentence after the signature). Where Originals in the Hungarian National Archives, MNL OL, E 190 (Rákóczi family archive), not seen. Used here in print: Szilágyi, Monumenta Hungariae Historica , Diplomataria XXIII (1874) nos. CIII and CXXIX, and Patera, Jana Amosa Komenského korrespondence (1892) nos. CLII and CLIV. Item 474 of the project’s catalogue of open ciphers. The cipher A reciprocal letter substitution (a↔m, b↔i, c↔p, s↔t …) inside clear Latin, word division kept. The same table is printed in MHH XXIII p. 740 as the secret script of Rákóczi’s envoys at the Porte. How it was deciphered The August sentence was deciphered in print by Szilágyi (1890) and Patera (1892). WAINUT transcribed both passages and rebuilt the key from that decipherment; the review found the key printed in 1874: all 12 letter values agree. What it says Nihil certius quam Poloniam periisse, et papatum in illa : “nothing is more certain than that Poland has perished, and the papacy in it”, written as the Swedes took Great Poland. Still open The 24 May passage (50 letters and three numbers), the word (iyy) , and one letter of the August sentence that the key reads as m where the decipherment has a . Credit WAINUT (pull request #102, 27 October 2026): transcription, key rebuilt and checked, attacks on the May passage. Adolf Patera (1892) and Sándor Szilágyi (1890) printed the decipherment; Szilágyi printed the key table in 1874.
comenius1655.html#letters

In 1655 Comenius was at Leszno (Lissa) in Great Poland, bishop of the Unity of Brethren, and a correspondent of the Rákóczi court at Sárospatak, where he had taught from 1650 to 1654. He sent news of Poland, Sweden and England to Andreas Klobusiczky, the prince’s councillor and prefect of Sárospatak, and through him to George II Rákóczi, whom he was urging towards an alliance with Sweden. Constantin Schaum, Rákóczi’s secretary, was then travelling to Sweden, Denmark, Holland and England on the prince’s business, and his letters came back by way of Comenius. (This background is not from the letter and was not checked against a source here.) Five letters to Klobusiczky survive from May to September 1655. Szilágyi printed them in Monumenta Hungariae Historica XXIII (1874) and again, with notes, in Erdély és az északkeleti háború I (1890); Patera printed them in his edition of Comenius’s correspondence (1892). Two carry a letter cipher: letter Patera 1892 MHH XXIII 1874 secret text 20 May CLI, pp. 177–178 none; the April letters to be read “as the Schaum papers must be, by agreement” 24 May CLII, p. 178 CIII, pp. 178–179 cipher passage, not deciphered 22 July CLIII, pp. 179–180 secret phrases and an invisible-ink page (section 05) 4 August CLIV, p. 182 CXXIX, pp. 217–219 cipher sentence, deciphered in print 6 September CLV, pp. 182–183 secret phrases, printed in clear (section 05) The originals are in the Rákóczi family archive of the Hungarian National Archives (MNL OL E 190). They were not seen; everything here rests on the page images of the printed editions, read on archive.org.
comenius1655.html#aug

The letter of 4 August reports the surrender of Great Poland to the Swedes, the army Comenius saw at Poznań, the flight of the Catholic clergy and the seizure of their goods. It ends Tuus totus , with no signature, and under it, as both editions print it: The end of the 4 August letter in Patera’s edition, with the cipher sentence and, at the foot of the page, his note: Značí: Poloniam periisse et papatum in illa (“It means: …”). Image: A. Patera, Jana Amosa Komenského korrespondence (Praha 1892), p. 182, with footnote *, via the Internet Archive (bub_gb_xnVMAAAAYAAJ, leaf n204). Nihil certius quam Cyhyqbma cgzbbttg, et CmCasda 69 655 m. The first three words and et are clear. Szilágyi’s note of 1890 (p. 393) gives the decipherment first: A titkos jegyekkel írt utóírás így hangzik , “the postscript written in secret signs reads: nihil certius, quam Poloniam periisse, et papatum in illa”. Patera repeats it in 1892. Neither says who deciphered it. Laid against that decipherment the cipher gives a key sign by sign ( check.py ): cipher sign by sign plain Cyhyqbma C=p y=o h=l y=o q=n b=i m=a a=m poloniam cgzbbttg c=p g=e z=r b=i b=i t=s t=s g=e periisse et clear et CmCasda C=p m=a C=p a=m s=t d=u a=m pap m tum, printed papatum 69 6=i 9=n in 655 m 6=i 5=l 5=l m=a illa One letter does not fit. Cipher a is plain m in poloniam and at the end of papatum , but the fourth letter of CmCasda is also a , so the key gives papmtum . Both editions print a there (checked on the page images). Either the writer slipped into the plain letter, or the printers read an m (cipher m = plain a ) in the hand as a . The word can only be papatum , and the printed decipherment has it; the conflict is kept visible in the reveal below. Two controls show the key is not fitted to noise: a shuffled key gives ltptnman lremmuur et lalnion is illa , and the right key on letters shuffled inside each word gives nolmioap rispeesi et pmautmp in lali . Nihil certius quam Poloniam periisse, et papatum in illa. “Nothing is more certain than that Poland has perished, and the papacy in it.” The cipher hides the one sentence that draws the conclusion from the news above it. Near the end of the same letter the clear text has a single odd word: Mire angitur bonus vir (iyy) de tantis sibi injectis remoris , “the good man (iyy) is wonderfully troubled by the great delays put in his way”, just after news of Schaum. MHH sets iyy in italic, as it sets cipher; under the key it gives boo , which is not Latin. It may be a misprint or a code name, and stays open.
comenius1655.html#key

The values above form pairs: a stands for m and m for a , s for t and t for s . WAINUT noted this and called a reciprocal table a guess. It is in print. At the very end of MHH XXIII, after the glossary, Szilágyi printed “the key of the secret script used by Harsányi and Máté Balogh”, Rákóczi’s envoys at Constantinople: “A Harsányi és Balogh Máté által használt titkos írás kulcsa”: the Rákóczi envoys’ table, a reciprocal substitution with f doubling for u / d . Image: S. Szilágyi (ed.), Monumenta Hungariae Historica, Diplomataria XXIII (Budapest 1874), p. 740, via the Internet Archive (okmnytriirkczyg01gygoog, leaf n724). All twelve letter values rebuilt from the August sentence agree with it ( check.py : 12 of 12). So Comenius was writing in the Rákóczi court’s own table, which Klobusiczky had at hand, and anyone with the 1874 volume could have deciphered the sentence; Szilágyi, who printed both, may well have done so for his 1890 note. The digits. The printed table has no digits, yet the printed sentence has 6, 9 and 5 for i , n and l . In the table those letters are b , q and h , and a hand’s b , q and h are easily taken for 6, 9 and 5. 69 655m is very probably bq bhhm as the printer read it, and the cipher a plain reciprocal table without digit homophones. Patera’s text of these letters follows MHH, so one misreading would appear in both; only the original can settle it.
comenius1655.html#may

On 24 May Comenius quotes, “in these words”, a friend’s letter from England of 23 April: Schaum had not yet arrived; the Polish and Swedish envoys in London; the Waldensians and Cromwell; the fleet in America. Then comes the cipher, in italic in both editions, then a postscript, Tandem appulit, cum has clauderem, dominus Schaum , which answers the English friend’s “not yet” and so seems to belong to the quoted letter. The cipher may therefore stand inside the English letter. MHH printed this letter as by “the Rákóczis’ Polish correspondent”; Szilágyi identified it as Comenius’s in 1890. The 24 May passage in Patera’s edition. MHH has the same letters, except Xyoapus for Xyopatus ; the italic long s and f cannot be told apart. Image: A. Patera, Jana Amosa Komenského korrespondence (Praha 1892), p. 178, via the Internet Archive (bub_gb_xnVMAAAAYAAJ, leaf n200). Lmqſxmyo. 7. Gpdlmuoyqnotlses: Pnofeyprp 865, ap 73 pyſ: pdyp: Xyopatus etc. etc. Fifty letters of seventeen kinds and three numbers, word lengths 8, 16, 9, 2, 3, 4, 8. It does not decipher: The Rákóczi table gives hantkaoy … ecuhadyonqyshtgt cqyvgoczc … cot cuoc koycmsdt . Read with the digit shapes of August, 865 would be ?il , perhaps nil , but the words around it are not Latin. With Caesar shifts added before or after the table, on 23-, 25- and 26-letter alphabets, and scored in Latin, English, German, Hungarian and Polish, the best result is −4.9 per character against −1.7 for the August plaintext. Keyword ciphers (Vigenère, Beaufort, Porta with about 10,000 Latin keywords and the names in the letters) and affine and progressive shifts, run by WAINUT: nothing. Annealing a simple substitution scored with the shared Latin model: a Latin control of the same length is recovered exactly, the May passage gives nonsense (−3.1 to −3.5 per character). A homophonic version, letters and digits as signs, cannot recover its own control at this length, so its output tells nothing either way. So the passage is not this table and not a simple substitution of Latin with the word division as printed. It may use another key, perhaps the English correspondent’s, or hide names, numbers or a reference; the colons and the closing etc. etc. look more like a list or a title than a sentence. The language of its plaintext is not known.
comenius1655.html#other

The catalogue entry spoke of four letters with ciphered sentences. Two of the others carry secret text of other kinds, and Szilágyi’s 1890 edition prints more of it than Patera: 22 July. The phrases et ad principem , non mitto ob securitatem and occultiora pagina sequenti, carbo ostendet were in secret script (“the words in italic were secret”, Szilágyi p. 392). The “more secret things on the following page, which charcoal will show” were in invisible ink, and Szilágyi printed what could still be made out after the page was held to the fire: Londino 4. Junii Constantinus Schaum. Non satis dici potest, quam grata fuerit protectori notitia mea … , Schaum’s report from London that Cromwell had received no more welcome message from any prince. The remaining twenty-five lines or so were already washed out. 6 September. A numbered list of questions for the prince, citing Drabík’s revelations by date, with the sensitive words ( Quid princeps agat , legatus Svecicus , Bisterfeldius , septentrionalibus jungi , Turcae …) in secret script. Both editions print them only in clear, in italic; the ciphertext is not printed.

The 24 May passage, all 50 letters and the numbers 7, 865 and 73: no key in print or in the editions’ notes; the original is needed to check the readings ( Xyopatus or Xyoapus , long s or f ) and to look for a key. papatum (4 August): the fourth letter is a in both prints, m under the key. The letter is taken from the printed decipherment and the sense: grade I for that one letter, H for the rest of the sentence. The digits 6, 9, 5 as misread b , q , h : a hypothesis from the printed table, not checked on the original. (iyy) : three letters, boo under the key; open. 22 July: the invisible-ink page beyond its first lines, illegible since at least 1890. 6 September: the secret-script passages exist only as the editors’ plaintext.

A second cipher enclosure to the nuncio in France (DECODE R73), on a princely marriage and again on Henri III and the nun. George Lasry recovered its key and decrypted it in 2020; 1,040 of its 1,082 groups have a value in his file. The record’s attachments date it to Como’s letter of 8 August 1580 and hold a contemporary clear copy of its second half, which agrees with Lasry’s text. 9 200^ 28 50 46 16 92 144^ 266^ 822^ 44 18 22 12 24 26 · non l a u d a M.S. che V.S. t e n g h i · (Lasry’s key) Rome → Paris · homophonic cipher of two-digit figures with nomenclator · 8 August 1580 · existing decipherment The Cardinal of Como to the nuncio Anselmo Dandini, 8 August 1580 from Cardinal Gallio Go to the full text ↓ The papal Secretariat writes to its nuncio in France about a princely marriage and about Henri III and a nun; George Lasry recovered the key and decrypted it in 2020. Measured on the words of the reading, the enclosure builds coherent sentences but reads at 88.5%, under the 95% bar. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (96% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · George Lasry (earlier solution) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (96% of the cipher) The letter Tolomeo Gallio, Cardinal of Como, papal Secretary of State, to Anselmo Dandini, nuncio in France: the cipher enclosure (“mezzo foglio di cifra”) of his letter from Rome of 8 August 1580. Where Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 283C ff. 89r–90r. DECODE R73, “partially decrypted”, with no date; catalogue item 244. The cipher Two-digit figures for letters, every second digit even, with one or two forms for the vowels; three-digit groups closed by a mark for words and titles. How it was deciphered George Lasry recovered the key and decrypted the transcription in 2020; both files are on DECODE. This page takes his text as it is. What it says A marriage proposal the Pope would take up only on good grounds; then the nun: the nuncio is not to raise her with the Queen Mother, and any reproof of the King must come from the Pope, quietly. Still open 32 illegible groups and six nomenclator groups without a value. Found here The date, from the covering letter, and a contemporary clear copy of the second section on f. 91, which agrees with Lasry’s text. Until 14 October 2026 this enclosure shared a page with R72, Como’s enclosure of 16 May 1580. That one keeps Lasry’s frame and nomenclator but reassigns the letters, a different key, with its own page .

Francia 283C holds the Secretariat’s original letters and ciphers to the nuncio in Paris for 1580. R73 is three pages of figures, ff. 89r–90r, on damaged paper with heavy bleed-through. DECODE gives it no date. The record’s attached images supply it: ff. 88 and 92 are Como’s clear letter, signed “Il Car.le di Como” and dated “Di Roma a 8 d’ag.to 1580”, with the note “Con mezzo foglio di Cifra” under the signature; f. 91 is a clear text headed “Cifra … dal S.r Car.le di Como con l’re di 8 agosto 80”. It is a decipherment of the second section of R73, on f. 90r. f. 90r, the first lines: 9 200 28 50 46 16 92 144 266 822 …, which Lasry’s key gives as non lauda M.S. che V.S. tenghi proposito alcuno… Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 283C f. 90r, via DECODE R73.
dandini1580r73.html#cipher

Lasry’s key (DECODE attachment D3190, 24 October 2020, filed on R72) is deterministic. Letters are two digits whose second digit is even: a 50 92, c 14, e 18 52, i 26 62, l 28, n 22, o 34 72, r 40, t 44, u/v 46 82, and so on; there are no nulls. Nomenclator groups are three digits followed by a mark: 124^ S.S. , 824^ N.S. , 822^ V.S. , 144^ M.S. , 224^ S.M.tà , 266^ che , 200^ non , 366^ per , 800^ mente , 966^ tanto , 988^ essere . His decryption (D3191) is KaJo’s 2017 transcription with a value under each group. Counted in his file, 1,040 of the 1,082 groups have a value (96.1%). The rest are 32 groups the transcription marks illegible, six occurrences of nomenclator groups he left without a value (866^, 466^, 766^, 324^, 300^, and 744^, which his key lists as egina without the mark), and four groups he marked with a question mark.
dandini1580r73.html#reading

The first section, f. 89r, concerns a princely marriage. In Lasry’s text a gentleman has spoken to the nuncio (“N.S. è certificato che il gentilhuomo … ha parlato”), and the Pope “sarebbe … intieramente certa di muoversi con buon fondamento a trattare la pratica”. The second section, f. 90r, is the nun, the affair of the May enclosure. The nuncio is not to speak of her to the Queen Mother, lest it give her cover to make a stir against the Pope’s wishes. The Pope has already acted through the King’s confessor; the King could do the same “ma è ben bisogno di procedere tanto circonspettamente che non ne nasca rumore né disordine alcuno”, and the reproof is to come from the Pope to the King. The clear copy on f. 91 gives the same section in the Secretariat’s words: f. 91: “Cifra … dal S.r Car.le di Como con l’re di 8 agosto 80”, then “Non lauda N.S.re che V.S. tenghi proposito alcuno con la regina m[ad]re nel particolare della monaca per non darle occasione di fare con tale coperta qualche rumore non conforme alla mente di S.S.tà …” Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 283C f. 91r, via DECODE R73 (attachment D1137). Compared by eye, line for line, the clear copy and Lasry’s text agree in substance. The differences seen: the clear copy has N.S.re where Lasry has 144^ M.S. ; darle where his values give parlio ; and regina madre where his file leaves 744^ open. The first section has no clear copy on the record.

R73, ff. 89r-90r, 8 Aug 1580 read in part Como to Dandini, cipher enclosure of his letter of 8 August 1580. f. 89r concerns a princely marriage negotiation; f. 90r the nun affair: the Pope does not want Dandini to speak with the Queen Mother about it, lest it give cover for some disturbance contrary to his mind, and the reproof should be moved by the Pope with the King, proceeding so circumspectly that no rumour or disorder arises. Decryption is George Lasry's (DECODE D3191, 2020, on KaJo's 2017 transcription D1789). Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (88% here); the holes are marked in the reading. [?diffusamente], sarebe S.S. intieramente certa di moversi con buon fondamento a tratare la pratica; però […] f. 90r Non lauda N.S. che V.S. tenghi proposito alcuno con la regina m[ad]re nel particolare de la monaca, per non darle occasione di far con tal coperta qualche rumore non conforme a la mente di S.S. Se da la parte de la monaca V.S. havese comodità di mezo tale spiritual, potrebe ella fare il medesimo con oficio simile a quello, ma è ben bisogno di procedere tanto circonspetamente che non ne naschi rumore né disordine alcuno, avertendo sopratuto che se questa monaca ne verà ripresa non sapia ella che la riprensione sia mosa et spinta da V.S. As to the part touching the King, as much is done as can be done with the office that Your Lordship performed about it with his confessor. If on the nun's side Your Lordship had the convenience of some such spiritual go-between, you could do the same with an office like that one; but it is very necessary to proceed so circumspectly that no noise or disorder of any kind arises from it, taking care above all that if this nun is reproved she should not know that the reproof was moved and pushed by Your Lordship. With the King, Our Lord would be well pleased if Your Lordship did some office openly about the dealing which you write is in the hands of brokers, to give away the church of Laon, putting before His Majesty part of the great deal that could reasonably be said on this matter.
