A homophonic solver (simulated annealing; 34 symbols to 26 letters, 150,000 steps, 8–12 restarts), first without and then with the word boundaries, on the target and on six matched controls: held-out French of 207 letters enciphered with a random key of exactly Pitt’s homophone multiplicities, adjacent words merged with probability 0.2 as in the target. run model controls read (of 6) target 1 5-gram, letters only, no word edges 0 (16–49 % right; the solver’s optimum beats the truth on 5 of 6) gibberish, 31 % of Pitt’s key 2 5-gram with spaces, raw corpus 3 at 99.5–100 %; 3 fall into an all- i attractor from OCR Roman numerals attractor 3 same, Roman numerals removed 5 at 99–100 %, one at 44 % −591.6 found against −602.4 for Pitt: a wrong key outscores the truth , 14.5 % agreement 4 same, training text with v → u , j → i 6 of 6 (98–100 %) 97.6 % of Pitt’s key blind : 202 of 207 tokens Run 1 repeats the Moray letter result at this length: 207 letters over 34 symbols with a plain letter-stream model is below the solver’s threshold even on controls, so a failure on the target would have meant nothing. Run 3 is the more useful one. The controls pass and the target fails, so the plaintext was out of the model’s distribution. The letter writes uotre, uie, uos, seruices, uoyes, subiet, ie , as every 1644 hand does; a model trained on a nineteenth-century edition with v and j scores that spelling some 200 nats worse than modern French of the same length, and gibberish wins. Normalising the training text fixes it. The recovered key differs from Pitt’s at three rare symbols only ( g , 14, e ), whose values n-grams cannot fix and the words do. The two 134-letter controls that were run under the same model (the tracker’s wrong length) both decrypt at 97–99 %, so the length was never the obstacle.

passage dated **13 May 1644** in the Richard Forster papers: ciphertext, proposed key, Python decoder, literal output, and an edited French reading with an English translation. **Earlier decipherments:** Karen Britland has informed Robert Pitt that George Lasry supplied a decipherment after publication of her article, and that Norbert Biermann independently reached the same solution. This project acknowledges their earlier work and makes no claim to the first decipherment. The supplied key decodes **207 encrypted tokens using 34 fixed symbol assignments**. Four letters require editorial repair in the readable version. This repository's specific key and editorial choices have not been verified against the handwritten manuscript or independently reviewed. ## Update — 15 September 2026 Britland's reply identifies the earlier work by **George Lasry** and **Norbert Biermann**. The reading she supplied agrees with the overall meaning of the reconstruction here, with some differences in wording: | Passage | Earlier reading supplied by Britland | This repository's edited reading | | --- | --- | --- | | Opening | `aucune voie de scrupule` | `aucun sujet de scrupule` (literal: `aucun subiet`) | | Prudence clause | `preveu seulement` | `prenez seulement` (literal: `prenez sdulement`) | | Final verb | `soupir` | `subir` (the supplied source plaintext also says `soupir`) | The reply did not include the earlier keys, working notes, or a manuscript image. It therefore provides evidence of prior decipherment and broad agreement in meaning, while the differences above and the four disputed cipher-derived letters remain unresolved. The original input, proposed key, and literal decoder output are retained for comparison. Source: Karen Britland's correspondence with Robert Pitt, reported by Pitt in this update. The correspondence is not a published source or a review of this repository's exact key. ## Files and reproduction | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | [ciphertext_source.txt](ciphertext_source.txt) | Supplied transcription, preserved unchanged, including existing plaintext and date. | | [recovered_key.json](recovered_key.json) | Proposed token-to-letter key and uncertainty notes. | | [decode_forster.py](decode_forster.py) | Deterministic decoder; applies the supplied key without editorial repairs. | | [decoder_output.txt](decoder_output.txt) | Complete literal output and numbered alignment of all 37 encrypted groups. | | [test_decoder.py](test_decoder.py) | Checks coverage, input validation, key use, and preservation of disputed letters. | Requires Python 3.9+ and only the standard library. From the repository directory: ```sh python3 decode_forster.py python3 decode_forster.py --alignment python3 -m unittest -v ``` Check that a fresh run exactly reproduces the committed output: ```sh python3 decode_forster.py --alignment | diff -u decoder_output.txt - ``` ## How the cipher and key work The proposed key is a **homophonic substitution**: each number or letter token maps to one plaintext letter, and several tokens can share a letter. For example, both `0` and `2` mean `e`; `4 30 q 30 19` gives `a u c u n` → `aucun`. Comma-separated groups can contain several words: `descrupule` is read as `de scrupule`. Word spacing within groups is editorial. | Plaintext letter | Cipher tokens | | --- | --- | | a | `4`, `p` | | b | `f` (tentative) | | c | `12`, `q` | | d | `7`, `a` | | e | `0`, `2` | | f | `70`, `n` | | g | `5`, `e` | | i | `16`, `d` | | l | `80`, `c` | | m | `u` | | n | `19`, `t` | | o | `s` | | p | `90`, `y` | | q | `88` | | r | `20`, `l` | | s | `40`, `x` | | t | `8`, `50`, `b` | | u | `30` | | y | `g` | | z | `14` | The two existing plaintext spans, beginning `ie vous en responds` and `et mesurer a cela`, pass through unchanged. The date is already plaintext. The decoder applies the supplied key; it does not automate recovery of the key. ## Edited reading These are this project's readings, incorporating the editorial choices documented below. They are not a transcription of Lasry's or Biermann's original working. **Modernised French** > Il n’y a aucun sujet de scrupule de manquer à Dieu ; je vous en réponds, et même > dans les règles de perfection. Prenez seulement les voies de prudence pour > conserver votre vie, pour en faire à Dieu un plus grand sacrifice, par la > multiplication de vos services pour le salut de vos frères, et mesurez à cela > s’il est meilleur d’agir ou de subir. > > 13 mai 1644 **English** > There is no reason to worry that you are failing in your duty to God; I assure > you of this, even according to the rules of spiritual perfection. Simply take > prudent steps to preserve your life, so that you may offer it to God as a > greater sacrifice by multiplying your services for the salvation of your > brethren. Judge by that whether it is better to act or to endure. > > 13 May 1644 ## Findings and uncertainties Four literal letters conflict with the proposed reading. Positions are numbered from 1 across encrypted tokens only, as in the output alignment. | Token position | Cipher → literal | Editorial repair | | --- | --- | --- | | 70 | `a` → `d` | `sdulement` → `seulement` | | 97 | `16` → `i` | `piur` → `pour` | | 103 | `q` → `c` | `conceruer` → `conseruer` | | 151 | `g` → `y` | `sacrifiye` → `sacrifice` | These repairs are confined to the edited reading. Changing the key globally would alter other occurrences of the same symbols. Their cause remains unresolved. - **Tentative assignment:** `f` appears once, at token 13. Assigning `f` → `b` produces `subiet`, a historical spelling corresponding to `sujet`. [Nicot’s 1606 dictionary](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Thresor_de_la_langue_francoyse_-_1606_-_1_-_Nicot.djvu/217) attests the spelling; it does not establish this cipher assignment. - **Additional editing:** `des uos` becomes `de vos`, omitting the `s` at token 174. The key always gives `30` → `u`; `u/v` and `i/j` distinctions, modern spellings, accents, apostrophes, and sentence punctuation are editorial. Examples include `subiet` → `sujet`, `reigles` → `règles`, `uoyes` → `voies`, `ie` → `je`, `responds` → `réponds`, and `mesmes` → `même`. The existing plaintext `mesurer` is edited to `mesurez`. - **Uncertain ending:** the supplied transcription ends with `soupir`. The [article abstract displayed by ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260410273_Reading_between_the_lines_royalist_letters_and_encryption_in_the_English_civil_wars) gives `soubir`. The edited `subir` / “endure” follows that variant and remains uncertain. This word is already plaintext and supplies no evidence for the key. - **Verification scope:** all 207 encrypted tokens are retained, every observed symbol is mapped, and the decoder applies no position-specific substitutions. Tests establish mechanical reproducibility. The archive’s 203/207 agreement with a proposed comparison reading measures internal consistency, not independently established accuracy or statistical confidence. The interpretation is counsel to preserve one’s life for continued service to God and one’s brethren. It does not identify the correspondent or establish a specific political event. The published passage may be only part of a letter; no missing text is supplied here. ## Sources and provenance Prepared from `forster_end_to_end_evidence.zip`. George Lasry’s 2022 key, published without a decipherment of these letters, was applied and extended. 95.1% of 2,477 letter signs decrypt to sense, measured; a dozen name codes stay open. ʃʃm → POUR · ✝ = Q · ɤ = D/T · ∽ = G · “POUR arrester ET traicter d’une levee de neuf mil suisses” [Guise] → the duc de Mercœur · homophonic cipher with a small nomenclator · 27 May and 20 June 1587 Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, May and June 1587 from Henri, duc de Guise → to Duc de Mercœur Go to the full text ↓ BnF français 15564 ff. 119 and 142 (DECODE R4162 and R4165): a page wholly in cipher and a slip with seven clear lines and sixteen of cipher. Both were decrypted with the key George Lasry recovered in 2022, which he published without a decipherment of either letter; the decryptions do not yet build sentences throughout, so both letters are decoded, not read. guise1587.html#f119

Decoded, not read. The letter was re-read on 23 October 2026 ( texts/f119_reading.md , with an English translation): the passages on the levies build sentences, but the opening lines and lines 5, 12, 25, 29–30, 33–34 and 37–38 keep unread runs, between homophones the context does not fix and name codes (24 of 43 sentences clean). In the manuscript’s spelling; […] marks unread signs, [?word] a doubtful word, [21] a name code. The passage on the levies: Nous avrons sans doubte deux mil lances italiennes ou albanoises et quatre mil reistres, soubs la levée de ce de [21], lesquels les leve pour nous. Il a envoyé son secretaire ve[…] vers [?le] colonel Fifer avec douze mil escus pour arrester et traicter d'une levée de neuf mil suisses, auquel nous n'avons eu encor response, et l'attendons a toutes heures. … L'armée des heretiques, de la grand et [?forte], et composée d'huict mil reistres, douze mil suisses, deux regimens de lansquenets, quatre mil harquebusiers pour Chastillon, leur doibt amener de cavallerie françoise ce qu'ils pourront. [?Je] vous diray que [?je] craigs trop plus les traistres que les ennemis, et le doubte for[…] si nous ne nous resolvons a nous en defaire, ce qu'est tant utile pour la gloire de Dieu et la cause que nous poursuivons. The Protestant army described is the German and Swiss force that the Huguenot party was raising in 1587 and which crossed into Lorraine in August; Châtillon is François de Coligny, the Admiral’s son, who led its French contingent. “Colonel Fifer” is Ludwig Pfyffer of Lucerne, the Catholic Swiss colonel who raised regiments for the League. The name codes [21], [43], [71] are not in Lasry’s key and are left as numbers.

BnF fr. 15564 f. 142 (Gallica, view 155): the clear news from Germany ends “… xy Suisses et xy lansquenets pour” and the cipher runs on from there. Dated below “Ce xx e Juing 1587”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 142, via Gallica btv1b9064027v view 155. The clear lines give news from Germany: the duke of Lunebourg with nine thousand horse will be on the Rhine by 20 July. The cipher, joined into running text ( f142_running_reading.md ; UPPER is a nomenclator group, [?] one unread sign, [x] a supplied letter), is decoded, not read: the middle builds, but unread signs and supplied letters fall in nearly every sentence (2 of 12 clean, 23 October 2026). The middle: la levee [de] mil lances et quatre mil reistres, qui est ung [i]nstable secours; et a si bien faict par des resolutions precipitees, nous sommes maintenant contrainccts [?] donner ordre a [n]os affaires, qui ne peuvent estre avec telles seurete[z] … si nos premiers desseings eussent esté effectue[z] avec ordre et mesure. [73] is probably a person the writer is to meet with troops at Meaux; the pronoun “la trouver” suggests a woman, perhaps the Queen Mother, who was negotiating with the League princes in the summer of 1587, but the code is not in Lasry’s key and the identification is not made here.
guise1587.html#method

Prior art. The DECODE records (created 2023) carry no key and no decipherment. Cryptiana’s page on Lasry’s BnF solutions lists ff. 27, 78, 119 and 142 under “Duke of Guise? in BnF fr. 15564 and fr. 15565” and gives the key table ( GL_BnFfr15564.png ) and the decipherment of f. 27 only. Transcription. Every sign labelled from Gallica full-resolution crops: 1,861 signs on f. 119, 623 on f. 142. Nomenclator groups (ff-ligatures for common words, digits for names) count as one sign. Decoding. Lasry’s key gives two to seven signs per letter, several of them near-identical shapes. A French language model (5-grams, fr-1600-letters ) chose among each label’s candidate letters and gave a first French text (about 70% sense). Fixing letters. About twenty passes of three lines each at 2× zoom, comparing each sign with the key and fixing the letter where shape and word agree; for the last runs, a search of the French corpora for phrases that fit the candidate letters (it found arrester , cherchions , en faisant estat , jusques icy ). Key extensions in this hand, beyond Lasry’s sheet: the hooked sign = D or “de”; ✝ = Q; ɤ = D, T or X; the x-shape = Y or N; 3/ʒ = C or D; 8 = M, B, N or T; the dotted Є = R; ʃ = A; “=ʃ” = P. Measurement. Each decryption file carries, per line, the number of signs and the number unresolved; the totals give 95.5% (f. 119) and 92.9% (f. 142), 95.1% of letter signs together. That counts signs given a letter, not sentences that read: the reading audit of 22–23 October 2026 found both letters decoded, not read.
guise1587.html#what-stays-open

121 letter signs of 2,477, scattered, no run longer than eight: each was retried in three or more zoomed passes and a phrase search. A few look like two-sign code groups (“98”, “89”, “z3”) rather than letters. Longest gaps: f. 142 line 1 (eight signs after “de”, including two ff-groups from Lasry’s unknown row), f. 119 line 3 (four), line 27 (“que [five] eschauffé”). Name codes: [21] (twice, a duke), [43], [71] (with “son frere”), [73] (twice, f. 142), [N], [&], [9b], and the groups ffv, ffσ, ffx, ffou. None is in Lasry’s table; each occurs once or twice. f. 119: unread runs in the opening lines and lines 5, 12, 25, 29–30, 33–34 and 37–38; the remaining choices are between homophones the context does not fix and nomenclator groups. f. 142: lines 0–2, 9–10 and 13 do not build, and the sign-level transcription was settled in 26 passes; no decipherment or clear copy exists. Grades: words in the full files marked with ? or in brackets are C or M; the identifications of Pfyffer and Châtillon are historical, not from the cipher.

huangxing.html

Three telegrams between Huang Xing in Tokyo and the anti-Yuan leaders at Zhaoqing, relayed by the Japanese Foreign Ministry, in which each telegraph-code number is written as three romanised kana. The cipher Each character’s four-digit standard telegraph code is written as three kana by a fixed arithmetic rule, and the kana are sent as romaji in ten-letter words. huangxing.html#documents

In May 1916 Huang Xing was in Tokyo and the provinces that had risen against Yuan Shikai’s monarchy had set up a Military Affairs Council (軍務院) at Zhaoqing in Guangdong. Messages between them went through the Japanese: the consul at Zhaoqing, Ōta, telegraphed them to the Foreign Ministry, which passed them on, and the Ministry filed copies. 20 May. Ōta’s telegram no. 42 of 21 May (B03050731100) forwards, at Cen Chunxuan’s request, a cipher text that his cover note says holds two telegrams: one from Cen and the provincial leaders, one “from Li Genyuan and others to Huang Xing” about the Xiehe army entering Hunan and Jiangxi. The same romaji, 126 ten-letter words ending owari , is copied a second time in the series on Sun Yat-sen’s circle (B03050089100, frames 0076–0078), where the Ministry’s analysts worked on it in pencil on frames 0079–0081 and got about 83 characters of the second telegram. Consul Ōta’s telegram no. 42, Zhaoqing, 21 May 1916: the end of the cover note (“the other is from Li Genyuan and others to Huang Xing … Chinese-side cipher follows”) and the start of the stream, sokahokaet arakotsuka atauichire , which decodes 黃克強先生鑒. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 1.6.1.75-1_015, JACAR Ref. B03050731100, image 24 (frame 0030), via JACAR. 25 May. Huang Xing’s answer went the other way. Foreign Minister Ishii’s telegram to Ōta of 25 May, 4.35 p.m. (B03050731500), asks him to pass on to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan a telegram from Huang Xing, “an acknowledgement of the telegram received the other day”. The cipher is on frame 0246, and the Ministry filed a cursive decode (frame 0247) and a clerk’s Japanese rendering (frame 0248) with it. Frame 0246: Huang Xing’s reply as handed in, five rows of ten-letter words ending OSOYUANIRA KISU. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 1.6.1.75-1_015 frame 0246, via JACAR Ref. B03050731500.
huangxing.html#cipher

The plaintext is the standard Chinese telegraph code, in which every character has a four-digit number (一 = 0001, 行 = 5887). Each number c is written as three kana. Tomokiyo found the rule and published it as a spreadsheet formula on 23 September 2026: kana rule table first S1[ c div 200] the 46 kana of the syllabary column by column: a ka sa ta na ha ma ya ra wa, i ki shi chi … wi, u …, e … we, o … ro second S2[( c − 1) mod 10] a i u e o ka ki ku ke ko third S3[(( c − 1) div 10) mod 20] ho he fu hi ha no ne nu ni na to te tsu chi ta so se su shi sa So 隱, code 7148, is RE-KU-TA, and 行, 5887, is KE-KI-NI wherever it occurs. The rule reaches code 9199, and a telegraph clerk who did not know it saw only pronounceable Japanese syllables. This project had looked at the reply in September 2026 without the rule. It found three kana to the character and that the same character always gave the same three kana, but took the code for a private code book. It also posited one superfluous kana, which was in fact a CHI misread as O-HI.

A decoder written here from the rule alone, with the repository’s own telegraph-code table, was run on the transcription of frame 0246 made here on 15 September, before the rule was known. With one change, Tomokiyo’s reading of O HI as CHI, all 46 groups decode: 隱印崧 詔鬯 行諸兄鑒：正 寄函 間，適接 哿 電，敬悉一切。護國軍能速入湘贑，甚好。行嚴何日東渡？望速啓行，先電示。興。 徑 “To Yin, Yin, Song, Zhao, Chang and Xing, brothers: just as I was sending a letter, your telegram of the 20th arrived, and I have noted everything. It is very good that the National Protection Army can move quickly into Hunan and Jiangxi. What day does Xingyan cross east? I hope he sets out soon; wire me first. Xing, the 25th.” 哿 and 徑 are the rhyme characters for the 20th and the 25th, and 徑 matches the date of Ishii’s telegram. The 1916 decode, corrected. Harumi-Matsuba pointed out (issue #48) that the cipher disagrees with the text this page gave in September, taken from the cursive decode on frame 0247. The decoder here confirms it from an independent transcription. The addressees are 詔 and 鬯, not 誥 or 蕘 and 邕; the second clause is 正寄函, not 正發書; and there is no 章 before 行嚴, which is an interlinear gloss on the decode and is not in the cipher. The text printed in 近代史資料 no. 50 agrees with the cipher on all of these, but lacks the 速 of 能速入湘, which the cipher and the Japanese copy both have. The six addressees are courtesy names: Lin Hu (隱青), Li Genyuan (印泉), Cheng Zikai (崧生), Wen Qun (詔雲), Yang Yongtai (暢卿, written 鬯) and Zhang Shizhao (行嚴). Harumi-Matsuba identified them from the 1916 staff lists of 軍務院考實; the footnote in 近代史資料 has four of them and other names for the fourth and fifth.

Harumi-Matsuba transcribed the stream with Claude from the JACAR images, compared it with four blind transcriptions by OpenAI Codex (94.6% letter agreement for the run made after the corrections), and decoded it with the same rule into 229 groups ( sankana-public , 20 October 2026). An earlier public audit of the same stream, saberwatchmanga’s sun-circle-cipher-1916 (10 October), found that the first telegram had been printed in 1916 and left the second unresolved. Telegram 1 , groups 0–107, the Council’s welcome. Printed in 1916 in 護國軍紀事 no. 5 as 軍政府歡迎黃克強電, so this is a check, not a new reading. The decoded text matches the print in 102 of 107 characters. The differences are 我, only in the print, and three places where the telegram reads 慮, 提挈公 and 查 against the print’s 憂, 教言 and 察: 黃克強先生鑒：奉删電，知公抵日，歡躍逾恆。堯等碌碌庸才，勉起討賊，正慮綆短，適逢公歸。願承不遺，俯賜提挈。公首倡共和，富有方略，各國情勢，考查復殷，將來內政外交，諸賴指導。大局所繫，惟公圖之。唐繼堯 岑春煊 梁啓超 劉顯世 陸榮廷 龍濟光 呂公望 蔡鍔 李烈鈞 陳炳焜 哿 Telegram 2 , groups 108–228, from six at Zhaoqing. No print has been found, and the continuous reading is new: 公抵日，喜甚。潤輔當告公近形，以定進行方略。軍務院僅擁虛名，委員、代表等會皆未組織。協和軍旬內可齊，卽由韶入贑。非俟幹卿協和兵入湘 贑 ，吾人恐難發言。馮段調停。此間暫置代理參謀事，源專任之。虎任第四 師 長，收集 舊部 約萬，亦卽出贑。 楷 調粤中湘軍卽 出 湘。釗擬來東，面達近情。虎、源、 楷 、羣、 泰 、釗。哿 “Glad you have reached Japan. Runfu will tell you how things stand here, so that we can settle our plans. The Military Affairs Council exists only in name: its committees and the delegates’ meeting are not yet organised. The Xiehe army will be assembled within ten days and enter Jiangxi by Shaozhou. Unless Ganqing and the Xiehe troops enter Hunan and Jiangxi, we can hardly make ourselves heard. Feng and Duan are mediating. For now the acting chief of staff’s duties here are given to Genyuan. Hu becomes commander of the 4th Division, gathers about ten thousand of his old troops, and also marches into Jiangxi. Kai will move the Hunan troops in Guangdong and march into Hunan. Zhao will come east to report in person.” The signatures are Lin Hu, Li Genyuan, Cheng Zikai, Wen Qun, Yang Yongtai and Zhang Shizhao, the same six that Huang Xing’s reply addresses. The consul’s cover note confirms that Li Genyuan was among the senders. Who “Runfu” is has not been settled, and Lin Hu’s title does not match later staff lists, which make him commander of the 6th National Protection Army.

A dropped or misread kana shifts every later group, so the stream as written goes wrong early. The two copies agree in 114 of 126 words, so most of the errors were already in the transmission. The corrections are listed with their reasons and certainty in the contributor’s corrections.csv . How far they can be trusted differs between the telegrams. In the first, the print was in view when they were made, so their agreement with it proves little; the fair test is the 59 groups that needed no correction, of which 54 match the print and the other five are the wording differences above. In the second there is no outside check except five spellings that the second copy writes as corrected. Its 43 corrected groups are graded M and the four inferred ones I ( underlined above where the reading is inferred or of medium certainty, as the contributor marks them).

Runfu will tell you of the recent situation, so that the plan of action can be settled. The Military Affairs Council holds only an empty name; the committee, the delegates' meeting and the rest are not yet organised. The Xiehe Army can be assembled within ten days and will then enter Jiangxi from Shao[zhou]. Unless we wait until Ganqing's Xiehe troops enter Hunan and [?Jiangxi], we fear we can hardly speak out. Feng and Duan are mediating. Here the business of acting chief of staff is provisionally arranged, [Li Gen]yuan taking it alone. [Lin] Hu is made commander of the Fourth Division, gathers his old units, about ten thousand, and will also go out into Jiangxi at once. [Cheng Zi]kai is moving the Hunan troops in Guangdong to [?go out] into Hunan at once. [Zhang Shi]zhao plans to come east to report the recent situation in person. Hu, Yuan, [?Kai], Qun, [?Tai], Zhao. The 20th.

Two intelligence letters from Rudolf II’s court, in clear French with short runs of figures. AngusRobinson recovered the key from the ciphertext with the probable word l’empereur : a homophonic figure substitution with 6 as the word space. Checked here against the images and a shuffle control, all 31 runs read, 534 of 536 tokens. Prague and Breslau → Duke of Nevers · numerical cipher · 1577 L’Abbé to Nevers, 1577 to Duke of Nevers Go to the decipherment ↓ BnF français 3198 nos. 30 and 37, with a second witness in no. 38. Imperial-court intelligence and Nevers’s business in mostly clear French, interrupted by numerical passages. The numerical passages were transcribed in draft and tested with substitution solvers under several hypotheses; no key was recovered and they are not deciphered. No earlier decipherment was found. The March letter reports a copy of the cipher sent on 24 February, the best lead to the key. The clear prose concerns imperial-court and Polish affairs, alongside l’Abbé’s correspondence with Nevers. Two details correct the earlier local outline: the opening describes l’Abbé’s own fever and nineteen days confined to his room; view 66 mentions 200,000 talers each year for the stated years for the Hungarian frontier. The full clear-text outline remains provisional and is not a diplomatic edition. On view 63, l’Abbé describes a recent cipher dispatch. The passage is in clear: Le 24e dudict passé j’escrivay au Sr Barquin [name provisional] par deux voies diverses […] et luy ay envoyé par l’une, copie de la chiffre que je vous envoyay avec mesdictes dernieres, affin que nous nous pouvions escrire librement. In substance: on the 24th of the previous month he wrote by two different routes and sent, by one of them, a copy of the cipher previously sent to Nevers, so that they could correspond freely. From the letter’s date this means 24 February 1577. Par l’une refers to one of the routes. The passage reports a dispatch; it does not establish that an enclosure survives or that both target letters use that exact cipher. BnF français 3198, Gallica view 63: the reference to sending the cipher. Bibliothèque nationale de France, via Gallica. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3198, Gallica view 63. The May letter’s clear prose concerns Nevers’s financial and legal business and a change of office at the imperial court. In the provisional reading, Weber has relinquished office before the emperor’s departure on 27 April, and Vieheuser has taken his place. The cipher follows a reference to Weber’s intention to attend the court for another two years. That context has not supplied its plaintext. The French word plusieurs is written in clear between the two numerical spans. Both copies retain the cipher, so comparing them helps with figures but supplies no independent decipherment. The working transcription of the clear prose and comparison of the cipher witnesses retain their uncertainties.
labbe1582.html#method

The draft transcription was extended from cached scans to every March insertion found. Solvers then tried different divisions of the digits into units, and possible nulls, scored with a language model of French letters. The cipher system is not determined. Division into one- and two-digit units by a fixed prefix rule, then constrained substitution searches. A first unrestricted homophonic search converged on repeated letters and was discarded. A sweep over ways of dividing the digits into units: 1,566 divisions passed filters on the number of distinct units and on leftover digits, and each was searched with three restarts of 5,000 proposals. Six fixed-pair variants and further point-delimited pairing/null treatments, including hypotheses about terminal sixes. A search on the May spans alone with a 5-gram language model, keeping the clear plusieurs and imposing the cribs mais…jamais and ne/ni . The cribs did not extend to coherent text, and none of their values is accepted. On a synthetic pair-substitution control the solver recovered all 538 letters. This tests the program only; it does not show that the historical cipher is of that type. An earlier attempt in this project reported a mismatch with the June 1580 “Chifre avec Madame”; the cached 1584 Nevers symbolic alphabet inspected here likewise supplied no numerical table for these letters. Neither comparison excludes every possible Nevers key. The experiment record identifies frozen inputs, programs, outputs and the corrected May test. French-looking fragments of solver output were not accepted as plaintext. Failures on an uncertain transcription do not show that the cipher cannot be broken. Independent solution by George Lasry. On 10 October 2026 George Lasry, working with ChatGPT Astra 6 and Anthropic Opus 5.5, deciphered the same letters independently from the ciphertext alone (526 of 533 elements identified, and all 43 of the duplicate) in his “BnF cipher research”. His reading of f. 75r, mais plusieurs ne pleureroient , agrees with the key from pull request #20. His other BnF results are listed on his contributor card .

Three cipher letters of January and March 1593 from Savoy’s agent in Paris during the League’s Estates General (BnF fr. 3983 nos. 11, 62, 100). Satoshi Tomokiyo had published the key and the images but no decipherment of these letters. His key was applied, corrected in about a dozen letter signs and extended with code values from glossed sibling letters; about 98% of the enciphered tokens have a value. ·26· δg4t ·85· 12 goooλm … [le duc de Mayenne] de [Monsieur] a esté remedié · 255 = tresve, 24 = l’Infante, 283 = lettres Paris → Turin · homophonic cipher with a 300-number code · January–March 1593 Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy: three cipher letters from the Estates of the League, 1593 to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy Go to the full text ↓ Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 3983 nos. 11 (f. 26, 17 January), 62 (f. 130, 10 March) and 100 (ff. 194–195, 27 March 1593). Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed the key from two letters deciphered at the time and published these three as images, with “many code groups yet undeciphered” and no decipherment of them. His key was applied here after a sign-by-sign transcription in three passes, corrected in about a dozen letter signs and extended with code values from the glossed sibling letters; about 98% of the enciphered tokens have a value. Measured on the words of the readings, nos. 11 (97.8%) and 100 (96.9%) reach the 95% bar; no. 62 builds coherent sentences but reads at 90.2%, under it. Lebel wrote to Charles Emmanuel I from Paris while the League’s Estates General met there to choose a Catholic king against Henri of Navarre. Fr. 3983 (Gallica ark btv1b9059406b) holds four of his letters in one cipher. No. 80 of 13 March was deciphered at the time on a separate sheet (f. 167); the other three are not. No. Date Leaf Gallica canvases Enciphered tokens (letter signs + codes) 11 17 Jan 1593 f. 26r–v 49–50 ~720 + 58 62 10 Mar 1593 f. 130r–v 233–234 recto 555 + 62; verso ~88 + 13 100 27 Mar 1593 ff. 194r–195r 333–335 890 + 110 (8 of the signs nulls) The system is a homophonic substitution of one or two signs per letter (a = pp or 12, e = Ɱ or g, o = # or ✱, s = ooo or 4t), three nulls (4+, X, o-f), a sign for et , and a code of about 300 numbers set off by dots, with an alphabetical addendum above 300 added later in 1593. Words are not divided. The counts come from the sign lists of the final passes. Grades as in the repository’s conventions: H a value in Tomokiyo’s key or glossed in a decipherment of 1593; C a value from alignment or several agreeing contexts; M a value inferred from grammar and sense in one context.

Translation no100_en.md # Lebel to the Duke of Savoy, Paris, 27 March 1593 (BnF fr. 3983 ff. 194r-195r, no. 100): English translation Translation (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026) of `no100_reading.md`. Code words resolved from the key or the contemporary glosses ({value} in the reading) are translated as plain words; `[?word]` translates a code value inferred from sense or queried; `[x]` letters supplied; `…` and `(?)` as in the reading. Clear and deciphered text are not distinguished. ## f. 194r On the 13th of this month I wrote to Your Highness, and I am still awaiting with good devotion Your Highness's commands, having received none since my departure, and even to hear that mine of the 25th of last month arrived safely, in which I repeated to you the principal points of what was contained in my letters of the 5th and 15th of January, which I believe were held up at Nevers. And in which I also told you that the lord has not made the credit over here that he wanted people to believe. He is very short of means. He has, in truth, lords and [?friends] among them. And he goes, as I believe, in good faith, having addressed himself to Your Highness because he foresaw that, if the first designs of the King of Spain could not succeed, Your Highness could with more reason than any other prince hope for much from this occasion, and that, making himself as it were the principal conductor of this negotiation, he could not but [?receive] from it much [?advantage], from now on and in the future, every good and advancement for himself and his people; so that I considered that what Your Highness would be willing to have given him from now on would be well employed. I told you the same with regard to his companion and the [?président] Jeannin, but that, as for putting great sums into [?their hands], I was not of that opinion; yet I have always thought, as I still do, that it is very requisite that Your Highness should have money brought at once to [?Paris], to do your service with it at need, without, however, the said lord knowing of it, who would not cease to [?press] for its disbursement. The [?Sieur] Zamet would be very suitable if he were willing to take charge of it. He is to come here very soon; I shall try ## f. 194v to discover his intention. For the rest, I shall tell Your Highness that it seems that [?God] is guiding affairs to the end which every good servant of Your Highness desires. The designs of the King of Spain for the Infanta, the prince(s) and himself are full of every impossibility. The favours I receive from the Duke of Feria and from the [?son] Tassis make me hope that, the said designs of the King of Spain being unable to succeed, it [Spain] may be resolved to do favour to Your Highness. And I have even learned that the said [?Commander] Tassis told a person that he believes it will have to come to that. The Cardinal Pellevé too let slip a word in passing that comes near it, and I am sure that Your Highness has not forgotten to have the required offices done with the Pope and [?the Legate / the Cardinals], being able to assure Your Highness that if the Pope, seeing that the designs of the King of Spain cannot succeed, inclined to do favour to Your Highness, you could not wish to have over here a better lord than the said Cardinal Pellevé will be to you, [?as I have] let Your Highness know by my other letters, as also that the procurators of the country of Provence and the Court of Parlement itself have written here to their deputies to beg Monsieur de Mayenne to give the government of the said country to Monsieur de Vaudémont; to which the said lord would not resolve until he knows Your Highness's will. The bearer and solicitor of the said letters is garre(?) well known, I believe, to Your Highness; he is of this town and lived a very long time at Marseille. Since I have been over here he has already made two journeys into Provence, and went back there not long ago. He always passes through [?Lyon]; if [?Monsieur de Nemours] were willing, [he could] make Your Highness a present of him. It seems to me that he would be very well lodged in the castle of Miolans. I am waiting from hour to hour for ## f. 195r [the m]an of the Friend, and by the same way some notable help, and leave to be able to make my way to Your Highness as soon as the assembly of the Estates separates, following the very humble request I made of it before to Your Highness, your service so requiring. The King of Navarre is resolving to harass and inconvenience this town more than ever, and has commanded all the neighbouring garrisons to let no more victuals come into it, whereby the dearness, which was extreme, will become unbearable to those who are not well provided with money for some months; which I beg Your Highness very humbly to take into consideration, especially as I have been living on loans these two months and can no longer hope for such accommodation. Monsieur de Mayenne is at the siege of Noyon, which he has battered with fourteen pieces; news of the outcome is expected from hour to hour, and it is believed he will carry it. The King of Navarre has ordered all the nobility of his party to mount promptly on horseback, and intends shortly to make himself the strongest in the field. Monsieur de Mayenne, leaving the siege of Noyon, will come straight here to attend the continuation of the Estates, when the Duke of Feria will come in to present his letters from His Majesty and make known to the assembly the continuation of his good will, then will ask the said assembly to appoint some to treat particularly with him; he is greatly astonished to find no one here [?devoted] to the [?greatness] of the King of Spain. [?As soon as] Monsieur de Mayenne has come, he will despatch [?someone] to Your Highness, having so written to me from the camp. By my first letters, which went astray, I advised Your Highness of a performance in the form of a dialogue which was recited at the lodging of Monsieur the Legate after the feast he gave the Princes, Princesses and other principal persons who were there. I send the text of it again to Monsieur Bruyset to send to Your Highness. ... [kiss] your hands very humbly, and pray the Creator to give you all contentment in perfect health. At Paris, the 27th of March 1593. (Postscript, left margin:) It is held that, when Monsieur de Mayenne comes back here, Monsieur de Guise will command the army. Eight code telegrams from the Portuguese head of government to the young King during his state visit to Spain, France and England. Maço 9 holds nine telegrams on eleven forms; the even-numbered images are mostly backs. Two are on Spanish palace forms (“Real Palacio”, Lisbon to Madrid, by hand): m0001, a clear text with four code groups, and m0003–m0004, all in clear. Seven are on French receiving forms with printed strips, Lisbon to Paris, Hotel Bristol; two of them run over two forms (m0011 + m0012, m0018 + m0016). Telegram no. 105, Lisbon to Paris, 27 November 1909, first three strips. Above the groups the receiver’s pencil: “com o Porto e Serpa assent ámos que …”. The six-figure 595191 and the four-figure 9581 are underlined as garbled. The year is not on the strips; the stamps read 27 NOV 09, and the dates fit together: m0011 is dated the 27th, a Saturday in 1909; m0009 (30th) complains of no answer to “Saturday’s telegram” and says the King leaves “the day after tomorrow”; m0007 (2 December) thanks him for agreeing. On four of the seven Paris forms (m0005, m0007, m0011, m0014), code items + clear words + a constant 9 for the address equal the taxed count of the header. m0020 gives 83, the figure the receiver pencilled over the header’s 93. m0009 is one short, and the office noted “(Correction suivra pour mot qui manque)”; m0018 is one short although its 91 groups were checked one by one.

Legião”. m0018: 69958 + 66931 are “tend-” + “-es”, i.e. “tendes feito”, the words of the King’s draft. m0020: 51443 is “contar com” and 19864 “isso” (one value, not two); 05068 “inconveniencia” and 19313 “posso” or “pouco” are doubtful. m0011: 48696 is “Hen..” (Hendaye?), and 43243 is left open there. lima1909.html#code

Pairing the glosses with the groups gives 261 distinct groups for 409 code items ( groups.py , code_values.tsv ). They are words, phrases (“com toda urgencia”, “depois de amanhã”, “dar ordens”, “resposta ao telegramma”), and syllables or endings for words not in the book (insis- / -to, Bri- / -and, estreit- / -amento, chega- / -ria, tornar- / -á). The code is two-part. Over 227 cleanly glossed groups, the rank correlation between group number and the alphabetical order of the value is 0.068, which 30% of 2000 random shuffles reach, and every first figure carries values from almost the whole alphabet. So an open group cannot be bracketed between its neighbours. Repeated groups agree: seven recur with two forms of one word or phrase (Em/em, teve/tem, terá/teria, comboio/comboios, relação/relações, 1 hora/uma hora). The one exception is 43243, “da” four times but glossed something like “dep..” in m0011. It is not the code of the neighbouring folders. No group is shared with King Carlos’s code of 1903, the Count of Sabugosa’s, Manuel II’s of August 1910 or Hintze Ribeiro’s of 1903. In this unit 38% of a telegram’s groups recur in the other seven, so a telegram of 54–106 groups in the same code would share some by chance; the chance of sharing none is below 2×10 −6 for each folder.

Telegram no. 105 of 27 November (m0011 + m0012), in the receiver’s decode; [?] marks a group not read or doubtful: Em combinação [?] com o Porto e Serpa assentámos que o mais conveniente seria tomar ahi o [?] da noite, 7 horas 40 minutos, com toda commodidade, tam bem ou melhor que [o] Sud-Express, e vir até Medina, onde teria comboio especial que chegaria a Lisbôa ás 11 horas [da] manhã ou mais tarde, se assim convier. Supprimia-se d’esta forma [a] paragem no caminho em Luso, incommoda e de mau effeito. […] Aguardando [?] Vossa Magestade para dar ordens, que são urgentes. W. de Lima. “In agreement with Porto and Serpa we settled that the best course would be to take there the [?] night train at 7.40 pm, in full comfort, as well as or better than the Sud-Express, and come as far as Medina [del Campo], where a special train would wait that would reach Lisbon at 11 in the morning, or later if preferred. This would cut out the stop on the way at Luso, which is awkward and makes a bad impression.” The other seven: m0001 (12 November, to Madrid): thanks for the welcome in Spain; “Tudo continua sem novidade. Escrevo Windsor.” m0018 (28 November): Lima edits the King’s reply toast for the President’s dinner: “e amizade” after “sympathia”, thanks for the welcome “na sua intellectual Paris”, “maior estreitamento das suas relações”. m0014 (28 November): since the President has given the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour to Bocage, the King should be friendly to Briand, with no inequality against what was done in England and Spain. m0009 and m0005 (30 November): no answer yet about the return trains; departure is the day after tomorrow; a stop at Bussaco would be awkward; Vasconcellos Porto presses for an answer. m0020 (30 November): the King should go only to São Carlos on the evening of his arrival and receive at the station. m0007 (2 December): arrival in Lisbon at 1.15 pm; greetings at Vilar Formoso; lunch between Santarém and Lisbon.

Three letters of 1586 in Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-2: Marshal Matignon’s report to Henri III from the siege of Monségur (BnF fr. 15572 ff. 218–219) and two autumn letters from Mayenne’s camp on money and an army breaking up (fr. 15573 ff. 120, 385). Harumi-Matsuba and Brett Burford deciphered them with Satoshi Tomokiyo’s key and Claude; 4,560 of 5,293 signs fall in runs of French, measured here, but no person has yet checked the transcriptions. + ∰ q X 9 δ x r 4 y gg a n s + ʒ 8 4 f 6 // T 23 … partira demain ou apres … ratrapera monsieur d’Halincourt Guyenne → Henri III · Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-2, homophonic signs with word signs · 1586 · known key applied, partial Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-2, 1586 from Jacques de Matignon → to Henri III Go to the full text ↓ Three letters from the royal armies in Guyenne in 1586, Matignon’s report on the siege of Monségur among them, deciphered by two outside contributors with Tomokiyo’s key: Matignon’s despatch builds coherent sentences but reads at 92.2% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs, the other two are decoded, not read, and none of it is yet checked by hand. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (40% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Harumi-Matsuba (solution, new cipher with solution) and Brett Burford (new cipher with solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · Also credited · George Lasry (earlier solution) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (40% of the cipher) The letters Marshal Matignon to Henri III from the camp before Monségur, May 1586. Two letters of autumn 1586 from the Duke of Mayenne’s side, sender not named; the cover of f. 120 (f. 121v) is addressed to Villeroy. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15572 ff. 218–219 and fr. 15573 ff. 120 and 385, on Gallica. ff. 218–219 were catalogue item 12 here; the other two were not in the ledger. The cipher Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-2: invented signs and figures for letters, signs for syllables and common words, and a slash between some words. It is not the Cipher-1 of the other Mayenne–Forget despatches. How it was deciphered Satoshi Tomokiyo published a table of the key. Brett Burford checked it on six letters in the same cipher that were deciphered at the time and added code values from them. Claude named the signs from the images, and the key was applied mechanically. What it says Twelve hundred shots against the wall of Monségur, three breaches, Sacramore de Birague wounded, an army short of everything and Mayenne in a fever. In the autumn, money that never comes and an army breaking up at the start of winter. Still open About 22 code signs, short stretches in all three letters (ff. 218–219 read at 92.2% of their words, measured 24 October 2026), and a check of the transcriptions by a person. In f. 120 and f. 385 the open stretches fall in most sentences, so those two letters are decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026). Credit The readings are Harumi-Matsuba’s (ff. 218–219 and f. 120, issues 49 and 51) and Brett Burford’s (f. 385, issue 46), October 2026, with Tomokiyo’s key. They were reviewed, spot-checked on the images and re-measured here.

Satoshi Tomokiyo (cryptiana, Henry III’s Cipher with Ambassadors ) distinguishes several ciphers in the papers of the Guyenne war of 1585–86 in BnF fr. 15572–15573. He lists these three letters as having no known decipherment and as written in the cipher he calls Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-2, and he publishes a reconstruction of its key. The project keeps one entry per key. These three letters are in Cipher-2, so they form this entry. The Mayenne–Forget despatches in Cipher-1 and Matignon’s slips in Cipher-3 have their own entries, and their code numbers mean different things. Tomokiyo’s table is a homophonic substitution: several invented signs and figures stand for each common letter. Other signs stand for syllables and short words such as de , la , que , est , pour and monsieur , and some figures for words, for example 23 apres , 24 peu and 31 pas . A slash marks some word ends. Burford checked the table on Mayenne’s letter to the King from the camp of Libourne, September 1586 (fr. 15573 ff. 103v–104r), whose decipherment of the time is written in the margins. He then read five more letters in the same volume that carry their decipherment (ff. 7v–8r, 32r–33r, 97r, 149r–150r). From them he took values for code signs: armée , tout , the ending -ée and 17 tant , and two more that he marks doubtful. Harumi-Matsuba used Tomokiyo’s table for ff. 218–219 and Burford’s key for f. 120. Two readings of the key still conflict between the contributors. For Harumi-Matsuba a barred h is armée , while Burford separates two similar signs, one tout and the other armée . A sign the table gives as q also stands where the decipherments of the time have pour .

The clear closing of the despatch on f. 219r, under its 19 lines of cipher: Sire, je supplie le Createur … Du camp devant Monsegur ce … May 1586 , and Matignon’s signature. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15572 f. 219r (view 226), via Gallica. Matignon wrote to the King from the siege of Monségur, which Mayenne’s army took in May 1586. The despatch opens in clear (the battery began at first light and lasted until sunset), and the cipher continues the story. Harumi-Matsuba’s reading begins: Et y ayant esté tiré pres de douze cens coups, mais ne feirent pas toutesfois tant d’effect que l’on s’estoit promis, parce que la muraille se trouva aussi beaucoup meilleure que l’on ne cuidoit. Three breaches were made, meant for a lodgement on one of them. The sieur Sacramore de Birague, on guard on that side, tried for it that evening, was badly wounded and had to fall back. Matignon held back the young nobles and now means to advance step by step. The army needs relief, as the sieur de Sailly has already reported. Something the cipher hides behind code 36 will have to come from Brittany to last until the harvest. The forces shrink every day, and pay matters most of all. The letter closes on Mayenne’s fever, which the physicians judge free of danger. This reading rests on a single pass by Claude over the signs. On six lines of another Cipher-2 letter with a known answer, the same method agreed with the decipherment on 74.8% of letters. A second transcription by OpenAI’s Codex, made without the first, agrees with it on 72–86% of values per page. The gist is secure, but individual words are not.
mayenne1586c2.html#autumn

f. 120 has no clear text in the cipher, but its cover survives as f. 121v, addressed “Pour Monseigneur de Villeroy” and docketed 1586 (found on the images, 23 October 2026), so the letter went to the secretary of state Villeroy. It is decoded, not read : the partial reading below rests on the decode, and its open stretches fall in most sentences. In Harumi-Matsuba’s partial reading, “this prince” is more vexed than ever. The treasurer Bilart has had thirty thousand écus in gold ready for ten days, and the Cardinal of Guise writes that five thousand are on the way. But “not five thousand but a hundred and five thousand” would not set the army right. The Marshal of Biron cannot be kept, deputies of the army have come, and papers of the secretary La Marsilière have fallen into “our” hands. The transcription was checked against an independent one by Codex (92% and 90% agreement on values), but not by a person. A word-by-word check of the reading against the decode (23 October 2026) restored the cipher’s own spelling and bracketed words only partly carried by the signs; recto lines 15–19 and 24–31 and verso lines 3–5 still do not hold, and one line checked on the image shows that finances rests on a look-alike sign. f. 385 , in Burford’s reading, describes the royal army in Guyenne breaking up as winter begins. Fewer than a thousand foot are left, men ask for leave, and there is no powder. The writer weighs what to do over the winter with the regiments and the foreign troops. He considers sending the landsknechts who were in Champagne and keeping a company of light horse, and he names Monsieur d’Halincourt, Monsieur de Matignon, La Roche and probably the young Aubeterre. Five passes of Claude were voted sign by sign, and on known text the voted reader got 93% of signs right. Burford’s v0.2 is itself a partial, unspaced decode; divided and punctuated here on 23 October 2026, it still has holes in most sentences, so f. 385 too is decoded, not read , and the account above is of its readable stretches only.

One measure for all three. Both contributors’ files were put in one format ( to_read.py ) and measured with the rule used for the Cipher-1 and Cipher-3 entries. A sign counts only inside a run of at least three words of a period lexicon ( fr-1600-letters ) totalling ten letters or more. The result is 1,856 of 2,138 signs for ff. 218–219, 1,002 of 1,103 for f. 120 and 1,702 of 2,052 for f. 385. Shuffled keys. With the letter values shuffled, 20 keys give medians of 10–16% per letter and at most 31%. Sense is not correctness. The measure shows the key turns the transcriptions into French. It does not show that each sign was named right, and the calibrations put that at 75–93% per sign. On the images. Here the line counts and layout of ff. 218v–219r, f. 120r and f. 385r were compared with the contributors’ files, and the clear closing and signature of f. 219r were transcribed. Three breaches were made, the plan being to lodge on one of them. - In the evening the sieur Sacramore de Birague, on guard on the side of the breach, went for the lodgement, was badly wounded and had to withdraw. The breach was defended from behind by a piece of wall that the guns had not brought down, and the lodgement was not taken. The defenders lost many of their best men; on this side some soldiers were lost and about twenty "b…" (with "…essés" at the head of f. 218v, read as blessés, the wounded: an inference). - The young nobles were held back. From now on, less firing and a step-by-step approach by lodgements. - The army is worn out and needs relief and provision for the future. The writer awaits the King's decision on how to use the army after the siege, on the Duke of Mayenne's proposals. - Something (sign 36, value unknown; guessed to be victuals, since it must last until the harvest) will be hard to find in sufficient quantity in the province and must be brought from Brittany. The forces shrink every day, and the troops not from the region want to leave. Most important of all is the payment of the troops. - The Duke of Mayenne has a fever, but the physicians are hopeful and there is no sign of danger. An American agent in Paris reported in code that Spain had ceded Louisiana to France. The Madison Papers printed the numbers with “key not found”. The one-part code was rebuilt here from four names spelled letter by letter (Lunéville, Parma, Tuscany, Dupont) and the alphabetical order of the code, and all 39 groups decode; the NARA microfilm confirmed a figure the decipherment predicted. 475.723.529.377.723.460.475.475.377 = L U N E V I L L E · 640.207.660.500.207 = P A R M A · 679 Spain · 434 France Paris → Secretary of State · one-part numerical code · 18 March 1801 · key recovered from the ciphertext Mountflorence to the Secretary of State, Paris, 18 March 1801 to James Madison Go to the full text ↓ An American agent in Paris reported in code that Spain had ceded Louisiana to France in exchange for Tuscany; the editors of Madison’s papers found no key, and the code was rebuilt here from the letter alone. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Founders Online (The Papers of James Madison) (transcription) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter James Cole Mountflorence, American consular agent in Paris, to the Secretary of State (addressed to John Marshall, received under James Madison), 18 March 1801. Two sentences in code, then clear news about prize cases and ships in quarantine at Malaga. Where NARA, RG 59, Despatches from US Consuls in Paris (microfilm T1), roll 1, frame 0097. Printed in the Madison Papers with the numbers undecoded: “Partly in code; key not found.” The cipher A one-part code of about 600 numbers in alphabetical order: single letters head each section, words follow. Names are spelled letter by letter, with full stops between the groups. How the key was found Two spelled names have telling patterns: nine groups ABCDBEAAD give LUNEVILLE and five groups ABCDB give PARMA. TUSCANY and DUPONT follow from the shared letters. The letters rise with the alphabet, so each word group can be placed between its neighbours. What it says On Dupont’s authority, Spain has ceded “the Mississippi, with all its Dependencies” to France, though not Florida, in compensation for Tuscany given to the house of Parma. Still open Nothing unread. Four common or bracketed words (Mississippi, but, at, the) rest on their place in the alphabet and the sense, and are marked [?]. The informant “Dupont” is not identified.

The coded sentences. The fourth group after “Compensation for” is 251. The Founders Online text prints it as 250, the figure that stands for “by” in the last line. Image: National Archives (NARA), RG 59, Despatches from US Consuls in Paris, microfilm T1 roll 1, frame 0097, via the National Archives Catalog. James Cole Mountflorence had been in Paris since the 1790s as chancellor of the American consulate and go-between for the American envoys. On 18 March 1801 he wrote to the Secretary of State, still John Marshall as far as he knew. The letter reached the department on 12 June under Madison and was docketed by Jacob Wagner. Its first paragraph is in code. The rest of the page is clear: the Council of Prizes would try no American ships until the convention of 1800 was ratified, and six American ships were in quarantine at Malaga. The Madison Papers abstract (Secretary of State series, vol. 1, p. 27) says “Partly in code; key not found. Coded section apparently discusses Louisiana cession.” Founders Online added a full transcription in 2015 with the numbers left as they stand. On 10 April 1801 David Humphreys, the minister at Madrid, told Madison that he could not decode a message from Mountflorence with the key the department had sent him. So the code was not the one Humphreys held.

This was done by some of the 666 secret Articles 228 at[?], 475.723.529.377.723.460.475.475.377 LUNEVILLE, as Compensation for 684.723.664.251.207.529.756 TUSCANY, given 250 by, 434 France, 719 to, 640.207.660.500.207 PARMA. I have it from very good Authority, Dupont, that Spain has ceded to France, not Florida, but the Mississippi, with all its Dependencies. This was done by some of the secret Articles at Lunéville, as Compensation for Tuscany, given by France to Parma. The report is accurate in substance. By the secret treaty of San Ildefonso (1 October 1800) Spain had agreed to return Louisiana to France in exchange for a kingdom in Italy for the Duke of Parma’s son. The treaty of Lunéville (9 February 1801) gave Tuscany to the house of Parma, and the convention of Aranjuez settled the exchange on 21 March 1801, three days after this letter. Spain kept the Floridas. Mountflorence, or his informant, places the cession in secret articles at Lunéville. “The Mississippi with all its Dependencies” is how he names Louisiana.

mountflorence1801.html#method

The punctuation gives the structure away. Groups joined by full stops form four runs of 6, 9, 7 and 5 groups, and each run is one word spelled letter by letter. The groups between commas are whole words. The nine-group run after “Articles” repeats in the pattern ABCDBEAAD. LUNEVILLE fits it once U and V are one letter, and the treaty of Lunéville, five weeks old, was the treaty that disposed of Tuscany. The last run, ABCDB, is PARMA. The run after “Compensation for” shares A and N with these and reads TUSCANY. The name after “Authority” then reads D-U-P-O-N-T from letters already known, plus two new ones. The fifteen letter values rise with the alphabet (A 207 … Y 756), so the code is one-part. Each word group must then lie between the letters around it: 679 between S 664 and T 684 is Spain (“679 has ceded”), 434 between E and I is France, 666 between S and Spain is secret, 432 just before France is Florida. 521 between M and N is Mississippi, 688 and 719 between T and U are the and to, and 228, 249 and 250 between A and C are at, but and by. The decipherment was first made from the Founders text, where 250 had to be both C (in TUSCANY) and “by”. That predicted a slip: the C ought to be 251. The National Archives microfilm, located at frame 0097 of roll T1-1, shows 251. The other 38 groups agree with Founders. No plaintext of the letter and no existing key were used. The probable words came from the history of the 1800–1801 treaties. The statistical check ( docs/_validate.py ) returns “too short” at 39 groups. What holds the reading is the alphabetical order of all 25 values, the cross-checks between the four names and the confirmed prediction.

All 39 groups have a value. The 27 letter tokens are fixed by spelling (grade S here, cross-checked). The 12 word tokens are grade I. Spain, France, secret and Florida are narrow: the slot and the sense agree. “To” is fixed by its two uses (“ceded to France”, “to Parma”); “by” is fixed by its slot between but and C. Weaker: 521 Mississippi (any word from Mi- to My- fits the slot; the sense asks for Louisiana by another name), 249 but , 228 at and 688 the , common words chosen from the slot and the grammar. “Dupont” is not identified. Pierre-Samuel du Pont de Nemours was in America at the time.

Two leaves of the volume, ff. 321 and 333, use a key of their own. Tomokiyo rebuilt it from f. 321 (La Rochelle, 11 June 1586), where the decipherer struck through every figure and wrote the clear text between the lines, and posted the table on cryptiana as a cipher of Henry III. The letter of f. 321 is addressed to Clervant, Buhy and Ségur as conseillers en mon conseil d’estat et surintendans de ma maison et finances : the king is Navarre. The same volume holds three letters of 1585–86 in another key of the same design, recovered from the ciphertext alone ( Navarre’s key A ), and a 1583 letter in a third ( f. 143 ). Each is a different cipher, with its own page; this entry was split from the key A page on 14 October 2026. Tomokiyo’s reconstruction of the f. 321 key. Bracketed numbers are syllables he inferred from the pattern; the decryption of f. 333 adds 24 = f, 34 = l, 36 = m and 61 = et. Image: S. Tomokiyo, Cryptiana (French Ciphers during the Reign of Henry III). The design is that of key A with the letters shifted by eight (a 12–14, b 15–16, c 17–18 … u 53–55, x y z 56–59, et 60–62) and rows for h and j added to the syllable table. In key A the figures below 12 are letters; here they are doubles and nulls, which is what separates the two keys at a glance.

f. 333 was transcribed at twice the working zoom from the full-resolution Gallica image: 108 numeric figures, 62 distinct, of which 103 take a value from the extended table. A free annealer on f. 333 alone (the method that recovered key A from 461 figures) does not converge: the best of twelve seeds has 35 of 58 letter figures right, and a matched control of the same size fails the same way. An annealer that builds in the chancery’s design (homophones in alphabetical order) re-derives the letter key blind, every seed agreeing, with 54 of 58 letter figures (93 %) as in Tomokiyo’s table, and 90 % on a matched control; the syllable rows are the weak part at this size. The reading itself rests on Tomokiyo’s key. f. 321 cannot be transcribed independently: the decipherer’s stroke runs through the middle of every figure, and removing it removes the digits. One clean segment, 61 130 33 78 54 52 = et si l fa u t , matches the interlinear et s’il fault .

The key records in the volume (R9257 Percy, R9260 Throckmorton’s first and second ciphers, R9261 Smith and Croft, R9262 Throckmorton’s third) do not match Norreys’s signs. A crib search against the Calendar’s wording was inconclusive: the groups are too short and too many words fit. The name signs did give three identifications, because they recur in the same order in the 9 and 24 February letters, and both Calendar entries run “the Protestants … the Prince [of Condé] … the Admiral”. The key came from Tomokiyo’s page on Elizabethan ciphers. Cabala (1663) prints Cecil’s cipher letters to Norris, and its “Postscript” to 27 September 1568 is really the decipherment of that letter’s cipher passages. From it Tomokiyo rebuilt a partial table. Signs may be turned in any orientation (⊏ = ⊔ = e, Γ = L = d), and single signs stand for persons. Applied to Norreys’s groups: Letter, item Reading Calendar 6 July 1567 (1) Master Stewarde “Signed: Stewart’s name in cipher” 4 June 1567 (6) #… Savoia … the in[t]e[n]d to ouerthrou # # a[nd] Engla[n]d “the King of Spain, the Emperor, with the Duke of Savoy intend to overthrow the Protestants of France, Flanders, and England” 10 July 1567 (2) the lord of Murrei … (rest garbled) “the Earl of Murray” 6 Feb 1568 (1)–(4), (7), (16) Leisly; [the] earl; Rothes ; papystes ; reaums (realms); stayid “one Lesley, brother to the Earl of Rothes, who came from the Papists of Scotland” 9 Feb 1568 (1), (3), (4) demaund ; reason ; peac[e] “whether now the demand of Calais were not very expedient … a mean to make peace” 9 Feb 1568 (5)–(9) the French King, the Protestants; ruin ; the Prince, the Admiral “peace betwixt the French King and the Protestants, otherwise Norris much doubts the ruin of the Prince of Condé and the Admiral” 24 Feb 1568 (2)–(4), (6), (8) the Protestants, the Prince, the Admiral; money; remain “the Prince and the Admiral … that they may have money to pay the Almains, whom otherwise he much fears will not long remain with them” Control. The script work/tomokiyo_apply.py counts dictionary words (the, and, lord, papists, realms, Rothes, earl, stayed, reason, ruin, master, steward…) in the decrypted groups. The real table gives 8 hits. With its letter values shuffled among the same signs (1,000 seeded trials) the mean is 0.22 and the maximum 3, and no shuffle produces a whole cribbed word such as Rothes, papystes, Steuarde, Murrei or Savoia. The table is Norris’s cipher, used from 1567 and not only in 1568. A word list, not a reading. Forbes copied only the ciphered words of the six earlier letters, so what the table gives for them is single words matched to the Calendar’s summaries, with no sentences to build. Under the reading bar the siblings count as decoded, not read (check of 23 October 2026); the word list stands as a word-level decipherment. Only the originals in TNA SP 70/96–97, whose clear text would put the words back into their sentences, could turn them into a reading.

A ciphered royal letter in the Koninklijk Huisarchief (G016-A0204) came with a clear version on a separate sheet. Rebuilding the key from the pair (letters near alphabetical order, vowels added as a cross or a dot on the preceding sign) confirms the clear version on the lines checked and corrects it twice. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 24 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Philip II to his half-brother Don Juan of Austria, “mi Capitan General de la Mar”, Madrid, 28 August 1574, signed by the King and countersigned by Antonio Pérez. Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Collectie Handschriften 2e serie, G016-A0204, two pieces, 6 scans on koninklijkeverzamelingen.nl. Catalogued as a letter in cipher to Don Juan “stadhouder van de Nederlanden”; in 1574 he was not yet governor there. The cipher Letters on one- and two-digit numbers in near-alphabetical order, with vowels added as marks on the preceding sign (a cross for e, a dot for i), a few code groups, and numbers written in clear. How it was checked The second piece is a clear version of the cipher. The key was rebuilt by aligning the two and then read back against the cipher line by line. What it says The King sends Don Juan the ransomed ensign Diego de Esquivia and, through him, letters encouraging Hürrem Bey, the Sultan’s chief interpreter, and a Milanese renegade engineer in Uluç Ali’s fleet to keep serving Spain. Still open Two code groups read only from context; about half the cipher lines not compared sign by sign.
philip1574.html#document

The item holds the King’s original and a single sheet in another hand. The original opens in clear, Ill.mo don Juan de Austria mi muy caro y muy amado hermano mio Capitan general de la mar , and then runs into some thirty lines of figures, with one clear phrase in the middle ( de lo qual los he querido avisar ). It is signed Yo el Rey and Ant. Perez and dated Madrid xxviij de agosto 1574 ; the address leaf and seal survive. The sheet gives the cipher passages in plain Spanish. Nothing on either says how the letter came into the house archive of Orange-Nassau. The opening. After Capitan general de la mar the cipher begins: 512 el , 2 12 7+ 19+ X alferez , 4 1 5 8 6 Diego . Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, G016-A0204, scan 1, via koninklijkeverzamelingen.nl. The clear version: El alferez diego de squivia ha venido aqui y hecho nos relacion de como fue cautivo de moros el año de 1558 . Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, G016-A0204, scan 2 (right-hand sheet), via koninklijkeverzamelingen.nl.
philip1574.html#cipher

At first sight the figures look like a code of two-digit groups. They are a letter cipher. Each consonant has a number close to its place in the alphabet counted with j and k (d 4, j 10, l 12, m 13, n 14, r 19, s 20, t 21, v 22; c 0, g 8, h 9, p 17, qu 18). The vowels have small numbers (a 2 or a looped sign, e 5, i 1, o 6 or 15) or are written as a mark after a consonant: a cross adds e, a dot adds i, a stroke above adds u. So 4+ is de , 18· is qui , and siendo alferez is 20 1 5 14 4 6 2 12 7+ 19+ X . X serves for both x and z, y is written g, and a few groups stand for whole words: pe como , co año , Lo carta . Years are left in clear with an overline (1558, 73). The full table is in key.md .
philip1574.html#reading

The ensign Diego de Esquivia, captured by the Moors in 1558 on the Count of Alcaudete’s expedition to Mostaganem, had spent years in Constantinople as a slave of Hasan Pasha, been freed in 1573 and gone to Naples to brief Don Juan. The King, having read his report, assigns him 15 escudos a month to serve near Don Juan’s person and asks Don Juan to employ him. Esquivia had also brought a letter from Hürrem Bey, interprete principal del turco , the Porte’s chief dragoman. The King answers it, animandole a la continuacion de nuestro servicio and promising him refuge in Spain if he has to flee; a second letter goes to Mostafa, ingeniero milanes renegado , who had been at La Goleta and now sailed with Uluç Ali in the Ottoman fleet. Esquivia carries both, and Don Juan is to decide how they are used. The letter is dated two weeks before La Goleta fell to that fleet. The clear text is in clear_version.md and an English translation in translation.md .
philip1574.html#check

About fourteen of the thirty-odd cipher lines, from the opening, the middle and both paragraphs, were deciphered with the rebuilt key and compared word by word. They agree, with two exceptions: The first paragraph ends que lo podra hazer in the cipher ( 9 ρ X+ 19 ); the clear version has saber . The interpreter’s name, which the clear version gives as [?]oran vey , is spelled in the cipher 15 19 ρ 13+ g , “Oram bey”: Hürrem Bey, chief dragoman of the Porte, who is known from other sources to have kept up contacts with Philip II’s agents. The clear version repeats de lo qual os he querido avisar ; so does the original, once in clear and once in cipher.
philip1574.html#open

Two code groups have one context each: 161 ( turco ) and g 90 ( Porque ). About sixteen cipher lines on scan 1 and the end of the cipher on scan 2 were not compared sign by sign; the clear version covers them. No other letter in this cipher has been found yet; the Philip II–Don Juan correspondence at Simancas would be the place to look.

Philip II to Don Juan of Austria, Madrid, 28 Aug 1574 (KHA G016-A0204) Philip II recommends the alférez Diego de Esquivia, a former captive of Hasan Pasha, to serve near Don Juan at 15 escudos a month, and sends through him answers to Hürrem Bey, the Sultan's chief interpreter, and to Mostafa, a Milanese renegade engineer with Uluç Ali's fleet, both encouraged to keep serving Spain. Decryption clear_version.md # The clear version (KHA G016-A0204, scan 2 right and scan 3 left) A separate sheet in another hand, headed "G16-A204" (modern pencil), with the text of the cipher passages of the King's letter. Abbreviations expanded in [brackets]; spelling as written. Paragraph 1 = the cipher block on scan 1 up to "de lo qual los he querido avisar"; paragraph 2 = the block after it. ## Paragraph 1 (scan 2 right) El alferez diego de squivia ha venido aqui y hecho nos r[elaci]on de como fue cautivo de moros el año de 1558 en la jornada que el conde de alcaudete hizo en berveria siendo alferez de la compañia del cap[ita]n ju[a]n de arcayda y del t[iem]po q[ue] estuvo en constantinopla siendo esclavo de azan baxa y de la manera que havia tenido liuertad el año de 73 y como havia venido a nap[oles] adonde vos entonces os hallavades a advertiros y daros noticia de algunas cossas que le parescieron convenir a mi servi[ci]o y al bien de n[uest]ras cossas de lo qual me dio una r[elaci]on muy particular diciendo q[ue] a vos os havia dado otra tal y haviendo se visto la dicha r[elaci]on y la buena narracion q[ue] da de todo lo de aquellas p[ar]tes ha parescido q[ue] por la platica y experiencia q[ue] tiene destas cossas sera bien serviros del cerca de v[uest]ra persona de lo q[ua]l os he querido avisar y para ello le avemos señalado 15 v[eint]e de entretenimi[ent]o al mes cerca de v[uest]ra persona de lo qual os e querido avisar para que lo tengays entendido y rogaros y encargaros mucho como lo hago q[ue] pues le conoceys y teneis noticia del le empleys y os sirvays del en lo que conforme a su qualidad y platica vieredes q[ue] lo podra saber ## Paragraph 2 (scan 2 right, continued) Porque el dicho Di[ego] desquivia nos truxo una carta de [?]oran vey (cipher: 15 19ρ 13+ g, "Oram bey" = Hürrem Bey, chief dragoman of the Porte) q[ue] dizque es interprete principal del turco y ha advertido que sera muy conveniente responderle a ella animandole a la continuacion de n[uest]ro servi[ci]o y offresciendole q[ue] si por esta caussa le fuere forcosso acudir a n[uest]ros reynos sera recogido y entretenido en ellos se le scrive en esta misma conformidad la carta q[ue] el d[ic]ho diego desquivia os mostrara originalmente al qual ha parescido entregarsela para que con v[uest]ra orden y conforme a lo que a vos os paresciere se sirva della y no de otra manera y assi sera bien q[ue] vos le ordeneys lo que en esto ha de hazer ## Paragraph 3 (scan 3 left) Anssi mismo se escrive otra carta a Mostafa q[ue] dizque es un ingeniero milanes renegado q[ue] ha estado en la goleta y aora anda con aluchaly en la armada del turco en la conformidad q[ue] el d[ic]ho diego desquivia ha advertido la qual tambien lleva el y os la mostrara para que se use della segun y como a vos os paresciere de madrid xxviij de ag[ost]o 1574 Translation translation.md # Translation of the cipher passages (from the clear version, corrected against the cipher) The ensign Diego de Esquivia has come here and told us how he was taken captive by the Moors in 1558 on the expedition the Count of Alcaudete made into Barbary, being ensign of the company of Captain Juan de Arcayda; of the time he spent in Constantinople as a slave of Hasan Pasha; how he gained his freedom in [15]73; and how he came to Naples, where you then were, to warn you and inform you of some things he thought fitting to my service and the good of our affairs. He gave me a very detailed account of it, saying he had given you another like it. Having seen that account and the good report he gives of everything in those parts, it has seemed that, for the practice and experience he has of these matters, it will be well for you to make use of him near your person, of which I have wished to inform you; and for this we have assigned him 15 escudos a month of allowance near your person. I have wished to tell you this so that you know it, and to ask and charge you earnestly, as I do, that since you know him and have knowledge of him, you employ him and make use of him in whatever, according to his quality and experience, you see he can do. Because the said Diego de Esquivia brought us a letter from Oram Bey [Hürrem Bey], who they say is the Turk's chief interpreter, and has advised that it would be very fitting to answer it, encouraging him to continue in our service and offering him that, if for this reason he were forced to come to our kingdoms, he would be received and maintained in them, he is written to in this same sense by the letter that the said Diego de Esquivia will show you in the original; it has seemed best to hand it to him so that he uses it by your order and as you think fit, and in no other way; so it will be well for you to order him what he is to do in this. Likewise another letter is written to Mostafa, who they say is a Milanese engineer, a renegade, who was at La Goleta and now goes with Uluç Ali in the Turk's fleet, in the sense the said Diego de Esquivia has advised; he also carries it and will show it to you, so that it is used as you think fit. Madrid, 28 August 1574. Key: key.md

Bourdeaux wrote to Maarten van der Goes, the Batavian Republic’s agent for foreign relations. The two DECODE images of R1944 carry about 110 numerical groups, each with a bar, tick, wave, dot or cross above the figures, then the closing “à bien respect” and his signature. DECODE records the nomenclator as numerical and “likely devised by S. E. Croiset”, the Dutch ministry’s cipher clerk. R1944, the cipher leaf stamped fol. 294.
