N°. 16. Berlyn 31 January 1801. De Heer van Rosencrantz verzekert de eigentlyke oorzaak van zyn renvoy te ignoreeren. Hy veronderstelt dat zyn Cyffer door middel van een bediende is genomen, en gecopieerd geworden, waar door dan zyne Gevoelens zyn bekend geworden. — Vry positiever meldt Lusy, dat het bureau, waar in zyn Cyffer was, is geforceerd geworden. — Het is om die reden, dat men den Heer Schuer, in N°. 13 gementionneerd, heeft willen naar Petersburg zenden om een nieuw Cyffer over te brengen. (get.) Bourdeaux Translation. Mr van Rosencrantz assures us that he does not know the real cause of his dismissal. He supposes that his cipher was taken by a servant and copied, and that his views became known that way. Lusi reports, much more definitely, that the desk in which his cipher was kept had been forced open. That is why they had wanted to send Mr Schuer, mentioned in no. 13, to Petersburg to carry a new cipher. The people are identified from context, not from print (grade C). Rosencrantz is most likely the Danish diplomat Niels Rosenkrantz, whom Paul I sent away from St Petersburg at the end of 1800. Lusy is Count Spiridon Lusi, the Prussian envoy there. Schuer is not identified.
r1944.html#remains

Every word of the clear sheet is legible (grade H). The cipher was not decoded against it: the groups have not been transcribed with their marks, and the key is not identified among DECODE’s key records. The clear sheet and the cipher share the number, the date, the sender and consecutive folios, so the identification is secure. A group-by-group alignment would also recover part of the key. Dispatch no. 13, which introduces Schuer, has not been located.

Inventory 337 of William V’s papers in the Huisarchief holds three DECODE records filed under the Hereditary Prince. Two belong together: R2237 carries ciphered observations with their contemporary decipherment, and from them the numbered word list was rebuilt that decrypts the Prince’s letter from Berlin of 12 March 1796, R2239 ( The Hereditary Prince of Orange from Berlin, 1796 , a different cipher, with its own page). The third, R2236, was catalogued with them. It is not in the same list. Copy No 1, the first lines: numbers between clear Dutch words (“op losse gronden”, “Echter schynt het als of”, “met een van beiden”, “De minister”). Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 337, via DECODE R2236 image 2 (rotated, contrast stretched). The four pages are “Copie No 1” and “Copie No 2”, copies of Dutch letters in which runs of numbers up to about 390 alternate with clear Dutch words, and a page of numbers up to 2835 that bleeds through onto R2237’s first page.
r2236.html#tried

The list that decrypts R2239 has about 250 entries, French words and phrases, many in alphabetical runs, and a group takes a whole entry, chosen letters of it, or the entry cut by some letters at the front or back. R2236’s numbers run to about 390, and to 2835 on one page, past that list, and its clear words are Dutch where R2237 and R2239 are French. So it is another list, or several. The other Orange ciphers of 1795 on DECODE (R1892, R2242) use a 6×6 square of digits, a different system again. The copies were viewed, not transcribed.
r2236.html#what-remains

Both copies and the page of numbers : not read. Blocker: no key material. No list or decipherment for this code was found on the record or in the file. A lead not followed: Karl de Leeuw’s article on Johann Friedrich Euler, cryptologist at William V’s court ( Cryptologia 25, 2001), cited on the DECODE records, may describe the Dutch lists. It is behind a paywall and was not seen.

The other leaves are a codebreaker’s worksheets, a household bill and a 1728 docket. Where British Library, Add MS 32287 ff. 37–40. DECODE R7707 listed it as a ciphered letter between unknown correspondents, dated by the volume span 1716–1836. Why it resists The index of coincidence is 1.07, which is flat and rules out a simple substitution in any language. Two hundred symbols are too few to recover a polyalphabetic key alone. How it was tried The signs were transcribed and the counts agree with the codebreaker’s tally on f. 40r. Monoalphabetic annealing in seven languages failed, as did Vigenère and Beaufort at periods 5 and 10 and a Quagmire-type search. Still open The text was not deciphered. Only outside material would help: the key, or the other letters named on the docket (31 August and 5 October 1728).

f. 37r, lines 1–4. On line 4, “8 5e 8” is written faintly. Image: British Library, Add MS 32287 f. 37r, via DECODE R7707. f. 37r : the cipher, ten lines, 205 signs, no word division. r7707.html#the-cipher

The transcription ( ct.txt ) uses arbitrary labels for the signs. Its counts match the 1728 tally within a few units for every sign: the commonest sign has 14 against his 14, and l has 13 against his 16. The “Duplicates” are simply the signs that occur doubled in the text. The index of coincidence is 1.07, where 1.0 is random. A monoalphabetic substitution of French or English would give 1.7–2.0. There is no repeated trigram in 205 signs. The periodic index rises slightly at periods 5, 10 and 15 (1.25, 1.34, 1.29). That hints at a five-alphabet system, but columns of about 41 signs are too short to prove it.
r7707.html#what-was-tried

Simple substitution by simulated annealing with the lang/ 4-gram models: English, French, German, Dutch, Italian, Spanish, Latin. The best was about −5.1 log-probability per letter; real text scores about −2.5. There are no words. Vigenère, Beaufort and variant Beaufort at periods 5 and 10. These took the order of the 1728 tally as the symbol alphabet. None gives plaintext. An unknown symbol alphabet combined with periodic shifts (Quagmire type), periods 5 and 10, French and English. None gives plaintext.
r7707.html#what-would-finish-it

Only outside material. That could be the key, or the other letters on the docket (31 August and 5 October 1728). More text in the same system would make a periodic attack feasible. The other DECODE records from Add MS 32287 (R7746–R7751) are Swedish keys of the 1830s, not this alphabet.

A letter and its annex in a plain numerical code reaching at least 1339, 303 groups (DECODE R1941). The archive inventory places them with the commissioners for the districts ceded around Zevenaar, writing from Düsseldorf. No key was found on DECODE or in print, and the text is too short for a ciphertext-only attack; not solved. 874. 729–. 821. 776. 826. 752. 1155. 956. 729–. 572. 58. 608 … key not found: a plain code reaching at least 1339 Düsseldorf → The Hague · numerical code · 14–15 January 1808 Van Spaen to Van der Goes, 14 and 15 January 1808 to Maarten van der Goes Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 2.01.08 Ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken 1796–1810, inv. nr. 281, DECODE R1941: a letter of two pages and a one-page annex, both in figures between clear Dutch openings and closings. Both items were transcribed from the DECODE images and the archive inventory was checked for who sent them. Every key reachable online was tested and none fits, so nothing was decoded. DECODE notes that the annex was deciphered, but no decipherment is on the record. The code has to come from the archive. C. van Spaen tot Voorstonden, “ambassador at the Court of Westphalia”, to Maarten van der Goes: a letter of 14 January 1808 (228 groups) and an annex of 15 January (75 groups), photographed twice. The inventory suggests the writers were the commissioners for the ceded districts around Zevenaar. Where Nationaal Archief, inv. 281 of 2.01.08; DECODE R1941, catalogued as partly decrypted (annex said to be deciphered, letter not). No decipherment is written on or attached to the record. The cipher A plain run of numbers from 15 to 1339 with no series marks, so not one of Croiset’s marked books. 222 distinct groups out of 303. How it was tried Every plausible DECODE key record was checked, Croiset’s 1803 codebook (R1035) gives word salad, and Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken V does not print the letters. Ciphertext-only was not attempted beyond counting. Why it resists With most groups occurring once, the letter cannot be decoded without the codebook. Still open No key has been found. The record owner’s decipherment of the annex would give about 70 values; the other route is the 1806–09 code of the ceded-districts commission.
spaen1808.html#the-documents

R1941, the letter of 14 January 1808 (DECODE image P3, from a photocopy): the docket, the clear salutation and the first five rows of figures. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 2.01.08 Buitenlandse Zaken 1796–1810 inv. 281, image P3 (from a photocopy), via DECODE R1941. The letter is docketed “Exh 14 january 1808” and opens in clear, “Hoog Edel Gestrenge Heer,”. Nineteen rows of figures follow. It closes in clear, “Ik heb de eer met de volmaakste hoogachting te verblijven, … Uwer Excellentie’s ootmoedige gehoorzame Dienaar”, with a signature read as “G. C. van Spaen”. The annex is headed “Dusseldorf den 15 January 1808” and filed as “136. Exh 18 january 1808”. It has seven rows of figures and the same closing. DECODE’s images P1 and P2 are two photographs of this one annex page. The archive inventory changes the attribution. In NA 2.01.08, inv. 281 is “Missiven van J.F.G. van Spaen en G. van Riemsdijk, commissarissen voor de overname der gecedeerde districten, de Lijmers, Huyssen, Malburgen en Zevenaar, jul 1806 – mei 1809”. G. C. van Spaen’s own letters as envoy in Berlin are inv. 244–248. The Düsseldorf letters therefore come from the Dutch commission for the territorial exchange with the Grand Duchy of Berg. Their subject is very probably that handover. A J.F.G. reading of the signature is not ruled out from the photocopy.
spaen1808.html#the-cipher

Each group is a number of one to four digits, separated by dots. A few groups are followed by a dash, which may mark a word boundary, and a few carry a small superscript letter ( 729 t , 793 s ), probably a clear ending as in other Dutch codes of the period. groups distinct letter, 14 Jan 228 181 annex, 15 Jan 75 69 both 303 222 Values run from 15 to 1339. The most frequent groups are 493 (six times), 297 (five), and 441, 424, 269 and 709 (four each). The sequence 602 441 373 occurs twice in the letter and once in the annex, and is probably a recurring name or title. Twenty-eight groups are shared between the two items. The transcription is targets/spaen1808/transcription.txt . In this hand 3 and 5 are hard to tell apart.
spaen1808.html#keys-tested

DECODE keys. Every key record at a Dutch holder dated 1780–1815 or undated was checked, then every key record mentioning Holland, Berg, Westphalia or 1806–10. None is for this code. Croiset’s 1803 codebook (R1035), applied to the annex, gives disconnected Dutch words. Both it and the 1798 book (R1891) use marked three-digit groups below 1000, which this code does not. The “solved” annex. DECODE’s note says the annex was solved, but the record carries no transcription or document file, and the neighbouring records R1936–R1948 are other letters. Print. The full text of Colenbrander, Gedenkstukken der algemeene geschiedenis van Nederland V (1806–1810), was searched for Spaen, Voorstonden, Dusseldorp and Westphalen. It prints nothing from these letters. Ciphertext only. Not attempted beyond counting. With 303 groups from a code of 1,300 or more values, most groups occur once, and no single solution is determined.
spaen1808.html#what-would-finish-it

The DECODE record owner’s decipherment of the 15 January annex. It would give up to about 70 values. If the code is alphabetical (one-part), those values would also bracket much of the letter. The code of the ceded-districts commission, 1806–09, among the Buitenlandse Zaken papers (NA 2.01.08) or the Van der Goes papers.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Sir Nicholas Throckmorton, ambassador in France, to Elizabeth I, Paris, 10 July 1559: his holograph, sixteen lines of cipher, signed. Where British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 32 (old f. 9), in the Forbes Papers; DECODE R2988 (with catalogue item 97, which DECODE listed as an unknown sender). The cipher Throckmorton’s first cipher: a letter alphabet of digits, letters and invented signs, with homophones, nulls and dotted signs for words and names. How it was deciphered With Satoshi Tomokiyo’s key for Cipher 1, attached to the DECODE record, after re-cutting the lines from the scan; seven values were corrected and four added from the text. What it says Throckmorton has already written twice on the 8th; he now sends a gentleman to report the French King’s state by word of mouth, asks the Queen to give him credit and to reward his “diverse and sundry” service, and signs off “at Paris the tenth of Julii”. Still open The reading audit of 22 October 2026 found the letter decoding only into phrases after its first sentence. Re-read on 23 October with the code signs on Tomokiyo’s key image, it now builds sentences throughout, but 30 of 496 letters in lines 5–15 rest on a choice between look-alike signs that no text of the letter can confirm, so it stays decoded, not read. Seven code signs not on the key, and a starred note keyed to line 13 that is written in a different code. Other ciphers The marginal text below the letter is a word-sign code with its own page ; John Wood’s 1568 line on the next leaf is another cipher, also with its own page . f. 32, the first four lines of the 10 July 1559 letter in Throckmorton’s Cipher 1. f. 32 (old 9) is Throckmorton’s holograph letter to Elizabeth, signed, sixteen lines of cipher in his first alphabet. Tomokiyo identifies the cipher and attaches his key to the DECODE record, but no decipherment of this letter was found in print: Forbes’s Full View does not print it, and the Calendar of State Papers Foreign has only the despatches of 8 July. Below and beside the subscription is a separate text in another system, the subject of its own page .

Key: Tomokiyo’s reconstruction of Cipher 1 (DECODE R2988 attachment), with these corrections: x and υ = i; y = f or h; z = m; ρ = d or t; ∫t and a flat-topped 6 = w; the looped Q = be ; ξ and dotted q = your Majesty ; a doubled sign and ζ inside a word are nulls. Code words are in square brackets; [..] marks not yet deciphered signs. The partial reading of 23 October 2026 ( texts/R2988_reading.md , English R2988_en.md ), in Throckmorton’s spelling; [?word] rests on a look-alike sign or on sense, […] is unread, and code signs not on the key are given by their shape: It may please your Majesty to be advertised that, whereas I sent [?letters] to the same by maister Gray of the eight of this moneth at five of the clock in the afternoone, and […] Carew [?letters] of the same date written at midnight touching the French King's state, […] I iudge your Majesty will be desirous to be further enformed thereof. […] then […] it […] conuenient to put in to writing the [?hoole] [?discours] of [1̲] [k̲], as I wish your Majesty to have knowledge of, considering the present [?time], have I iudged it best to dispatche this gentelman, to [?whom] [?I] enforme the same of the state of all [r̲] here at [?good] lenght, to whom it may [?please] your Majesty to giue credit. He [?hath] since [?his] coming on [?this] side done your Majesty diuerse and sundry wais so [?good] and [?painfull] seruice, as he [?hath] deserud to be well considered and rewarded, beseching your Majesty to be [?so] much [?his] [?good] and gracious lady, as he may perceiue [?his] seruice [?hath] bin acceptable, wherof I have had [?good] experience, as I shal be able to declare more plainli and particularly to your Majesty when it shall please the same to command me to attend upon your Majesty. And [v̲] I beseche [?God] to preserue your Majesty in health, welth and all felicite. […] Paris the tenth of [?Julii]. Grades (README Conventions): lines 1–4 H; lines 5–15 C where the key gives the letters, M for the bracketed guesses. On 23 October 2026 lines 5–15 were re-transcribed sign by sign at measured line centres (the “illegible” spans of September were crop overlaps) and decoded with the code signs on Tomokiyo’s key image, which the September passes had not used: as , have , had , whom , upon , so , this , and your Majesty , which is also the sign first taken as a null. The letter now builds into sentences, but 30 of its 496 letters (6%) rest on look-alike choices (ρ t / d , 7 r / g , μ h / b , x i / y ), more than a reading may carry, and no text of the letter exists to settle them: decoded, not read. The sibling letters in the same cipher (DECODE R2986, R2987 of 9 July and R2990 of 13 July 1559, which Forbes prints, I pp. 157–160) could settle the doubtful values: the next step. The two despatches of the 8th that it mentions are CSP Foreign I nos. 947 and 950; the bearer is not named in the deciphered part.

Seven code signs and groups not on Tomokiyo’s key list (1̲ k̲ in l. 6, a dotted t in l. 5, r̲ in l. 8, v̲ in l. 14, a barred l in l. 15, and two short groups in ll. 2 and 4); five of the twelve open in September are on the key image after all ( have , had , so , your Majesty , upon ). 30 of 496 letters in lines 5–15 resting on look-alike choices; the sibling letters of 9 and 13 July, checked against Forbes, are the way to settle them. The starred note keyed to the star in line 13: it is written in the marginal word code, which has no key ( the margin page ).

A one-page letter in Croiset’s six-series numerical word code (DECODE R2034), whose only copy is an undigitised booklet (NA 2.21.045/34313). Three 1801 letters in the same code with contemporary decipherments were transcribed and aligned: they fix 3 of the 67 words, and nine values claimed earlier are withdrawn. No other key fits; not solved. 430~ · 336~ · 501 · 1+ · 410 · 394 handen · … · 907^ · 222̅ niet · 43~ … 763~ end The Hague → St Petersburg · numerical word code, six series, Dutch · 30 Jul 1803 Lodewijk van Toulon to Dirk van Hogendorp, 30 July 1803 from Lodewijk van Toulon → to Dirk van Hogendorp Nationaal Archief, 1.02.13 Legatie Rusland, inv. 208; DECODE R2034. A single page from the Batavian foreign ministry’s cipher clerk to the Republic’s new envoy in Russia, in clear only at the date, the salutation and the signature. Its code is Croiset’s Correspondentiecijffer , which survives only as an undigitised booklet in the Nationaal Archief. No decipherment of this letter is known. Three of its 67 words were fixed from 1801 letters in the same code that have contemporary decipherments; the other 64 need the book. A start control (430~) and an end control (763~) enclose 67 text groups; 41 padding groups follow. Where DECODE. The key is a Correspondentiecijffer by S. E. Croiset, inv. 34313 of the Croiset papers (2.21.045) at the Nationaal Archief, not digitised. The cipher A code with six series of numbers from 1 to 992 (unmarked, or marked with wave, caret, double stroke, bar or plus), not alphabetical, with homophones. How it was tried The same code carried three Berlin dispatches of 1801 (R1944–R1946) with contemporary decipherments, transcribed and aligned here. They fix three of the 67 words: handen , brengen and niet . The codebook R1035 and the key R1038 were tested again and neither fits. Why it resists Too little is fixed to recover the other 64 groups. An earlier claim of nine values did not survive the full transcriptions and is withdrawn. Still open A scan of the six written pages of inv. 34313 would let the letter be decoded mechanically. R2034, the first five rows. Each group carries its series mark above it: a wave (430, 336, 51), a caret (120, 526, 307), a double stroke (897, 230, 934), a bar (528, 451, 877) or a plus (1, 518, 616). Unmarked groups are a sixth series. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 1.02.13 Legatie Rusland inv. 208, via DECODE R2034.
toulon1803.html#the-letter

DECODE’s cataloguer notes that a cipher clerk seldom wrote in his own name to an envoy, and that such a short message “can only pertain to matters of encryption”. The date fits: six days later, on 5 August 1803, the ministry signed a new and much larger codebook for the St Petersburg legation (DECODE R1035). Hogendorp’s own ciphered dispatches of 5 July 1803 (R1942) were written in the older code, the one Toulon uses here. The code has six series of numbers from 1 to 992: unmarked, and marked with a wave, a caret, a double stroke, a bar or a plus. The same number under a different mark is a different word. The 1801 decipherments show that common words have several equivalents ( Heer is 453̅ and 370~), and that the words in each series are not in alphabetical order (in the wave series 297 is Men , 370 Heer , 500 dat , 580 de , 733 zeer ). A number therefore says nothing about the word it stands for, and without the book only a word already seen in a deciphered letter can be decoded. The transcription was checked against the image at full zoom. Ten groups differ from the first transcription of 20 September: 336~, 897″, 880^, 859~, 528̅, 145^, 616+, 215̅, 625̅ and 188̅.

The key’s annotation says it was used “in anno 1801” with the Batavian ministers abroad. Three dispatches of the chargé d’affaires Étienne Bourdeaux from Berlin survive with their decipherments: R1946 (no. 20, 7 February 1801): 202 groups against a 158-word decipherment that opens “De Heer van Haugwiz en de Heer van Krudner, die intime vrienden zijn, zyn zeer en peine over het envoy van Kalitscheff naar Parys”. After the start control 357″ it runs strictly one group per word as far as niet (word 150). That fit is confirmed where 153̅ falls on Paul and 222̅ on niet . R1944 (no. 16, 31 January 1801; its decipherment is misfiled as R1946’s third image): 115 groups against 77 words. The subject is a stolen cipher. Rosencrantz believes a servant copied his cipher, the bureau that held it was broken into, and a courier is being sent to St Petersburg with a new one. 927+ is Cyffer three times, but two runs of the code have no counterpart in the decipherment. R1945 (3 February 1801): 187 groups against 152 words. The alignment drifts, so no value can be fixed from it. Every group of R2034 was looked up in all three, and in Hogendorp’s R1942, which has not been decoded. A value counts only if the number and the mark both match: Group Word of R2034 Value From Grade 394 5 handen R1946, word 111 H 58 28 brengen R1944, its last word M 222̅ 51 niet R1946, word 150 H 934″ · 907^ 18 · 50 wonderlijk · zoo Sillem’s paraphrase of R1942 I Three padding groups also turn up in R1946 (205̅ gantschelyk , 458+ ook , 239″ antwoord ). This confirms the code is the same but adds nothing to the text. J. A. Sillem’s 1890 biography of Hogendorp quotes “zo wonderlijk” from the ciphered dispatch no. 12 of 5 July 1803. The adjacent pair 907^ 934″ in R1942 is a plausible match, but nothing in the print fixes where the phrase falls, so the pair is kept only as a conjecture.

The nine values of the first pass. The 20–21 September pass put 51~ = van , 279 = en , 153 = Paul , 43~ = zyne , 304~ = wegens and 380~ = de . It took them from partial alignments of R1944 and R1946 that were never saved as transcriptions. The full transcriptions do not contain those groups where the table put them. In R1946 van is 444̅ or 957~ and wegens is 564~. Paul is 153̅ with a bar, while R2034’s 153 has none. These values are withdrawn. The 5 August 1803 codebook, R1035. Van Kampen’s reconstruction (HistoCrypt 2026) has 1,849 entries in seven series. R2034 was decoded with every assignment of its five marks to R1035’s six. The best assignment gives no more hits than random marks do (22% of groups under the natural mapping, 28% at random), and the words it produces do not connect. Its one striking run, “met Zijne Keizerlijke Majesteit”, is a single phrase entry between two empty cells. Hogendorp’s R1942 of 5 July is also at chance against R1035, as it should be for a dispatch written a month before that book. The 1765 St Petersburg key, R1038, and Schimmelpenninck’s key, R1891 (Croiset papers inv. 34312). R1038 has no entry for niet , handen or brengen . Both mark single digits rather than whole groups, so they belong to different systems. The other Batavian records on DECODE. R1926 (Schimmelpenninck, London, 28 February 1803) and R1896 use digit marks. R1947 and R2053 (Van Dedem, 1789) use four-digit groups. R1033 (Six van Oterleek, 1808) is in the R1035 book. None is in this code. Print. Sillem’s Dirk van Hogendorp (1890), the 1943 edition of Hogendorp’s letters to his brother, Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken IV, Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana and Van Kampen’s paper give no decipherment of this letter.

64 of the 67 text groups. None occurs in the deciphered 1801 letters, and a non-alphabetical, homophonic word code this short cannot be rebuilt from context. The book itself: Nationaal Archief 2.21.045 (Croiset), inv. 34313, old no. 5187. It is a ten-page booklet with six written pages and six loose sheets of notes, held as a photocopy; the original, Museum voor Communicatie B1 392, is also described at NA 2.21.227/335. A scan of it would allow R2034 to be decoded, and with it R1942 and Hogendorp’s other 1803 dispatches.

Two pages of three-digit code sent to Prince Carl August Friedrich of Waldeck, an Imperial and Dutch general, and dated by his French draft reply on the back to 18 January 1744. The 717 groups belong to a two-part homophonic nomenclator with no surviving key. Tested on synthetic letters of the same size and design, the language model rates wrong keys above the true one, so the letter was not deciphered. Ew. H. Dl. 524 . 99 . 916 . 38 . 442 . 692 . 447 . 90 . 507 . 24 . 22 . 402 . 924 . 556 = 863 . 888 . 119 . 382 . 92 . 42 . 84 . 9 . 465 . 4 . 341 . 937 . 19 . 227 . 298 … … the opening of f. 3r, after “Durchlauchtigster Fürst” Unknown informant → Prince of Waldeck · three-digit code · January 1744 · not deciphered Military news in code for the Prince of Waldeck, 1744 to Prince Carl August Friedrich of Waldeck Two pages of numbers sent to an Imperial and Dutch general in the War of the Austrian Succession, probably from a man hoping for a commission in his regiment; the code has no key, and one letter proved too short to rebuild it. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 28 September 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter An unsigned letter in German to Prince Carl August Friedrich of Waldeck-Pyrmont. His draft reply on the back answers a letter of 18 January, so it dates from January 1744. Where Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 118 a Nr. 3954, ff. 3r–4r, filed as “Militärische Nachrichten für Fürst Carl August Friedrich (in Chiffre)”; HCPortal record 517, “not solved”. The cipher 717 dotted groups from 4 to 999, 303 of them different. It is most probably a two-part homophonic nomenclator: a numbered list of letters, syllables and words in no alphabetical order, with several numbers for common entries. How it was tried The file, the Waldeck papers and the Marburg keys on HCPortal and DECODE were searched for a key. Letter, alphabetical and nomenclator solvers were each tested first on synthetic letters of the same size. Why it resists On a synthetic two-part nomenclator of this size, wrong keys score better than the true one. One letter does not determine the key. Still open The whole text. A key or a deciphered copy could be in the undigitised volumes on the 1744 campaign in the same fonds (118 a Nr. 1973–1980).
waldeck1744.html#letter

The file holds one letter on two leaves. Folio 3r is headed, in a flourished hand, Durchlauchtigster Fürst , then Ew. H. Dl. (Euer Hochfürstlichen Durchlaucht) in clear, then nineteen lines of numbers. A later hand has written “1744” in the corner. Folio 4 is a narrower leaf with twenty-six more lines. Ew. H. Dl. appears once more in clear, in its seventeenth line. There is no signature and no date. The back of folio 3 carries a docket that was never finished: “Schreiben an [blank] in Ziffern”. The opening of f. 3r. The first line ends 556.= with the German hyphen, so a word runs on to the next line and the code has units smaller than words. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 118 a Nr. 3954 f. 3r, via Arcinsys Hessen (image 0003) and HCPortal record 517. The back of folio 4 was used for the prince’s reply, drafted in French and corrected as it was written. It opens: “Je viens de recevoir, Monsieur, votre lettre du 18 e Janv.” He first thanked his correspondent “des nouvelles que vous me donnez et de tout le bien que vous me souhaitez à l’occasion du renouvellement de l’année”, then shortened the thanks to the New Year wishes alone. He asks for news “de chez vous” as often as possible. Vienna reports that the lieutenant-colonel will leave the regiment, and he promises to remember his correspondent when places fall vacant. The prince’s draft reply on f. 4v, written on the back of the cipher. It dates the ciphered letter to 18 January 1744 and shows its writer hoping for a place in the prince’s regiment. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 118 a Nr. 3954 f. 4v, via Arcinsys Hessen (image 0005). Carl August Friedrich (1704–1763) owned an Imperial infantry regiment from 1739. He was an Imperial Feldzeugmeister and, from 1742, a general of infantry in Dutch service. In 1744 he served with the Austrian army, and in 1745 he commanded the Dutch at Fontenoy. The writer’s place is not named. The prince’s interest in news “de chez vous” suggests a court or army he could not see from his own.
waldeck1744.html#cipher

The two pages were transcribed here from full-resolution crops of the scans: 45 lines, 717 groups, 303 of them different and 144 used once. The groups run from 4 to 999; 19 have one digit and 133 two. They are separated by dots, dashes or bare spaces with no pattern. The second leaf writes 2 as a z-shaped figure, and its 5 ends in a hook that can look like a colon. The commonest groups are 19 and 141 (14 times each), 38 and 341 (13), 24 (11), and 7 and 937 (10). Two features fix the kind of system. The sequence 879.144.X.126 occurs four times, with X = 90, 7, 7 and 924. In its second occurrence the writer began a 9, struck it through and wrote 7 above. These are several numbers for one entry, chosen at will: homophones. f. 4r, line 5: 879 . 144 . 9 7 . 126 . On f. 3r the same phrase has 90 in this place, and on f. 4 l. 20 it has 924. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 118 a Nr. 3954 f. 4r, lines 4–6, via Arcinsys Hessen (image 0004). Second, 303 different groups in 717 are too many for a letter cipher of the period, which gave each letter three to six numbers. A letter alphabet of about 130 numbers could not produce them. The table must also hold syllables and words, as the line-end hyphen already showed.
waldeck1744.html#system

A one-part code lists its entries alphabetically with the numbers rising, so its usage piles up where frequent German entries fall ( die , der , the e - and ge - syllables, und ). The share of text carried by each stretch of numbers was compared with that profile, built by encoding 1740s German with a sorted syllabary. Random numberings of the same counts give the baseline. Numbering tested Fit to German (lower is better) Random numberings Verdict alphabetical, 1–999 0.192 0.077 rejected letters in 1–99, alphabetical 100–999 0.149 0.077 rejected columns by last digit, as in the Hessen-Kassel keys of 1723 and 1720–30 (best of 20 orders) 0.057 0.047 no support multiplicative scrambling n = a·p mod 1000 (best of 400) 0.038 0.036 no support Nothing in the numbering behaves alphabetically. A two-part design fits: letters with about four scattered numbers each, some six hundred syllables and words with one number each, as in the Hessen-Kassel key of 1730 for Hanoverian correspondence (HStAM 4 d Nr. 1229). A synthetic letter encoded that way gives 310 different groups, 146 used once, a commonest group of 14, and 93 groups used three times or more carrying 429 tokens. The letter to Waldeck has 303, 144, 14, and 85 carrying 425. It departs only in its heavy use of numbers under 100, which fits a clerk who took the first number listed for an entry.
waldeck1744.html#tried

A language model of 1740s German was built for this letter from 202 texts of 1724–1767 in the Deutsches Textarchiv: Berlin newspapers of 1737–41, the Hamburgischer Correspondent and military manuals, 23.6 million letters. Every solver was run first on synthetic letters of the same size whose key is known. Attack On the synthetic control On the letter Letter-by-letter homophonic annealing (5-gram) Gibberish scores as well as or better than the true text Best score in the same range, no two runs agree The same with a dictionary word score added True key scores highest, but 12 runs of 20 million moves and heat-bath sampling stop short of it — Alphabetical-table annealers (after the van Swieten solve), with letters free under 100, column orders, heat-bath sampling True key highest only at a low letter bonus; searches stall below it Fragments of words, no sense Two-part nomenclator assignment True key −1284 against wrong keys found at −255 (bonus 1.0), −1934 against −1060 (bonus 0.6) Not run: the control shows the answer would not be identifiable The last row settles it. For a two-part code of this size, the language model rates many wrong keys far above the true one, whatever the allowance for longer units. A search that reached the true key could not recognise it. The probable New Year wish cannot be used as a crib either, because in a two-part code the unit boundaries are unknown.
waldeck1744.html#search

No other cipher item is catalogued in the Waldeck cabinet papers (118 a) or in any Waldeck fonds after 1646. The two older Waldeck ciphers, of 1638 and 1646, are simple letter substitutions. HCPortal’s Marburg records and its 319 keys have nothing for Waldeck in the 1740s. DECODE lists 112 Hessen-Kassel keys of 1710–1799 from Marburg; the German ones examined (4 d Nr. 1229, 1231 and 1237) do not fit this letter. The volumes where the correspondence of January 1744 would sit are not digitised. These are 118 a Nr. 1973–1980, “Akten betr. den Feldzug von 1744” (volume 1 covers January to May), the prince’s wartime correspondence (Nr. 1969–1972, 2044) and the officers’ applications of 1745–1750 (Nr. 2047). The prince’s reply shows that his chancery could read the letter. A deciphered copy, or the key itself, may survive among them.

E 199 is the Wesselényi family archive in the Hungarian National Archives; the leaf also carries an older number, “E 199 IV/3.t.–1”, and the archive’s stamp. DECODE photographed it together with the next item in the folder, R675 (8. pallium 1. 02), a Hungarian letter headed “NB Rottal” in a different number cipher. The images are not in the public domain, so none is reproduced here. The page is written in one hand. The cipher words sit inside Latin sentences, each number followed by a point. Three corrections show a draft being written: the writer put 14 twice in millia and struck one; he wrote “tandem aliquando necessario” after nux , struck it, and wrote it again a line lower after durissima ; and he struck a word after accommodari . A letter as sent would not look like this, so the page is Wesselényi’s own copy, which is why it is in his family’s papers. The heading at the top of the page (“S…zzi”?) is not legible.
wesselenyi1664.html#the-cipher

The alphabet is numbered backwards from 24, on a 24-letter alphabet that has w and no j or v: 24 a · 23 b · 22 c · 21 d · 20 e · 19 f · 18 g · 17 h · 16 i · 15 k · 14 l · 13 m · 12 n · 11 o · 10 p · (9 q) · 8 r · 7 s · 6 t · 5 u · (4 w) · 3 x · (2 y · 1 z) and four more numbers double the vowels: 25 a · 26 e · 28 o · 29 u (27, presumably i, does not occur). Numbers in brackets are not used on this page. The two numbers above 29, 60 and 64 , stand for a person and a place. DECODE key R672 (MNL OL P 1238, Teleki Mihály collection, cipher keys no. 12, dated 1660–1690) has exactly this alphabet, from 24 = a to 1 = z. After it come syllables in fives, 25–29 Ba Be Bi Bo Bu up to 115–119 Za…Zu, and names from 120 (Rex Pol., Turca, Imperator, Cassovia…). This letter does not use that syllable table: here 25–29 are bare vowels, and R672’s 60 = Ka and 64 = Ku give no sense in “Dominus Generalis [60]” or “ad [64] in castris”. The two are related keys, built on the same alphabet, not the same key. The writer made one slip. Spork is written 7 9 11 8 15 , and 9 is q; p is 10 everywhere else on the page ( praesidium , sponte , acceptare , temporis , peditum ).

Cipher words are in bold. Spelling as written ( presidium , Snaidau ); cleartext transcribed from the image, with (?) where a clear word is doubtful. Castrorum(?) mutationes etiam necessariae essent, quo facto, si Dominus Generalis [60] regimenta Dominorum Haster, Snaidau et Spork coniungeret, possent ad minimum tria millia hominum constituere , quibus si adiungerentur adhuc duo millia peditum , ut cum illis nos ad [64] in castris collocaremus, quam necessitatem videns [64] forte promptius presidium Maiestatis Vestre reciperent . Quod si vero illud sponte et benevole acceptare nollent , extunc de ulterioribus faciendis actionibus temporis occasioni nos accommodari debebimus, quia hoc est certum(?), quod ista nux durissima tandem aliquando necessario frangi debet. Alioquin non esset bonum, si hoc modo ab indusio quoque nostro timere et formidare deberemus. Translation. Changes of camp would also be necessary. That done, if the Lord General [60] were to join the regiments of Messrs Heister, Schneidau and Sporck, they could make up at least three thousand men; and if two thousand foot were added to them, so that with them we might take up camp at [64], then [64], seeing the necessity, might more readily receive Your Majesty’s garrison. But if they would not accept it of their own free will, then for the further actions to be taken we shall have to fit ourselves to the occasion of the time, for this is certain: this very hard nut must at last, of necessity, be cracked. Otherwise it would not be good if in this way we had to fear and dread even our own shirt. Haster and Snaidau are the imperial colonels Heister and Schneidau, spelled by ear; Spork is Johann von Sporck. All three commanded regiments in Hungary in the Turkish war of 1663–64, which ended with the peace of Vasvár in August 1664; the draft belongs to that war rather than to the later years of DECODE’s span. Indusium is an undershirt: to be afraid of one’s own shirt.
wesselenyi1664.html#method

The starting point was DECODE’s transcription of 2020, in which the transcriber wrote some figures as letters (b for 6, g for 9, i for 1, o for 0). Checked against the photograph, it needed one correction: the run after prius opens with 10, not 20. That gives 244 cipher tokens of 27 kinds. Three solver runs were tried with the project’s shared 4-gram models. With no limit on homophones, the Latin model filled every slot with i, because the model rates runs of i highly. A strict one-to-one key could not fit Latin at all (25 numbers, a 21-letter Latin model), and on Hungarian it gave text that only looked like Hungarian. With at most two numbers per letter, all eight Latin runs returned the same readable text with a few slips ( teneralis , castorsnaidae ). Those were fixed by hand from the clear context: si Dominus … generalis gives g e n e r a l i s, and tria millia hominum sets 17 = h. The names, nux (3 = x) and ab indusio were decrypted last. To check the key and look for 60 and 64, the neighbouring DECODE records were fetched: R675, the Teleki collection keys R665–R673, and the keys of the Vienna conspiracy file (HHStA Fasc. 327 Konv. D, R676–R690). Each was scored against the recovered values. Only R672 agrees, on 19 values. None of them gives the two codes a sense.
wesselenyi1664.html#what-remains-open

Code 60 , once: “Dominus Generalis [60]”. A person, the general in command in the sector. Wesselényi’s drafts of 1664 press de Souches’s army, which makes Souches the likeliest name, but nothing on the page proves it. Grade I at best; left open. Code 64 , twice: “nos ad [64] in castris collocaremus”, “videns [64] … reciperent”. A place whose people might take an imperial garrison, and the “hard nut” of the next sentence. No key found. Doubtful values, grade M: 26 = e occurs only once, in Haster (it is R672’s “Be” slot, and only e gives a name); the slip 9 for p in Spork . All other letters are grade H. In the clear text, the first word ( Castrorum ?), certum (?) and the heading are uncertain readings of the hand. They do not affect the cipher.

The Earl of Manchester’s papers at the Beinecke (OSB MSS fc37) include a run of letters from Robert Yard at Whitehall in September and October 1699, while Manchester was ambassador in Paris. Yard writes most of each letter in clear and puts names, places and the matter of each sentence in numbers, from a single group to runs of twenty, in the middle of the English. Two letters of the run carry a decipherment written between the lines at the time they were received: 28 September/9 October (box 2, folder 39) and 5 October (folder 45). The next two, 12 October (folder 49, two pages with an endorsement “Mr Yard 12/24” on the third) and 16 October (folder 51, two pages), have no decipherment on them. The Beinecke catalogue describes both as “almost entirely in cipher, undeciphered” . The Historical Manuscripts Commission’s 8th Report, Appendix II, p. 74, calendars them in the same terms and adds that “No key to the ciphers of the period is known to exist among the State Papers”. Yard to Manchester, 12 October 1699, p. 1, from on my part. The to and there : 241.120.128.356.211.112.286.10.316.126.476.327.347.1038 is messengers stayes yet at Dover , and the line ends in clear, looking . The V -shaped figure in V3 and V317 (lines 6 and 7) is one of Yard’s two ways of writing 2. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, OSB MSS fc37, box 2, folder 49, p. 1, via Beinecke IIIF 16601219. Satoshi Tomokiyo had already identified the code. His cryptiana page on the ciphers of the period lists the Yard letters from the DECODE database (R2858–R2860), says that the two without a contemporary decipherment (R2859, R2860) “can be deciphered with THE=454”, and decodes the first few groups of each. No full decoding of them was found online; Cole’s 1733 Memoirs were not checked (see below).

Box 18, folder 47 of the same collection is a large printed sheet endorsed “Copy of the E. of Manchester’s Cypher”. It is a one-part code template of fourteen columns, each running A to Z: first the single letters, then two columns of syllables, then words and names in alphabetical order. The printer set only the plaintext; the numbers were written in by hand, one to a slot, from 3 up to 2342. The hand skips every number ending in 5 or 9, and jumps from 516 to 617. In the T block the second syllable column reads tr 450, tl 451, ty 452, th 453, the 454, tru 456. The key, rows S–V of the first columns: printed syllables and words, handwritten numbers. the is 454; the numbers run 124, 126, 127, 128, 130 and never end in 5 or 9. Some blank slots have been filled by hand ( Sixty 867, Seven 1027, Sixteen 1028). Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, OSB MSS fc37, box 18, folder 47, via Beinecke IIIF 1213691. A note at the foot of the sheet gives the rule for the nulls: “The numbers under 3 and above 2342 and All numbers ending in 5 and 9 are Blanks. As are likewise the numbers between 516 and 617”. Blanks means nulls. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, OSB MSS fc37, box 18, folder 47 (foot of the key sheet), via Beinecke IIIF. All 1,456 numbered slots on the recto were transcribed, in 25 tiles from the full-resolution image. Three entries sit in a fold and cannot be read (1584, 1744, 1904). In practice Yard also uses the slots that are numbered but carry no word as nulls: 322 , 482 , 740 , 742 , 900 , 902 , 972 , 1060 , 1062 , 1854 , 2190 , 2236 , 2258 , 2278 , 2291 , 2317 , 2336 , 2342 . The decipherer of the 5 October letter passes over 740, 900, 2172 and 2278 in the same way. Yard’s key was not numbered exactly like the copy at Yale, because the numbers on each copy were written in by hand. Three differences show in the letters: 42 and 48 are e , not f as on Manchester’s sheet: sent three is 281.667.453.117.42.48 , se-nt-th-r-e-e . 21 is d , not c : Drummond’s ends 87.21.123 , n-d-s . Both values agree with the reconstruction in HMC’s Addendum 141a (48 = E, 21 = D), which Tomokiyo had flagged as not matching the printed sheet. 483 is and though the sheet prints ard . Tomokiyo notes that Vernon used it the same way. Yard writes the figure 2 in two ways, one of them shaped like a V , so V3 is 23, V17 is 2317, V34 is 234, V36 is 236.

Whitehall, 12 October 1699 I have the favor of your Lordp’s letter of the 7/17 of this month, and am sorry I could not effect what your Lordp desired in your letter of the 3d Oct. I hope at an other time your Lordp will be able to give me earlier notice, and I assure you nothing shall be omitted on my part. The messengers stay yet at Dover looking for Mills . I hope wee shall meet with him at last . Wee have an account from the Lords Justices of Ireland that they have received private information that many disaffected persons return dayly into that Kingdom , and that there is some ill design against the Government . The like intimations come from the north that some thing is designed in Scotland , and there the same intimations likewise with relation to England . And all is said to be carryed on very privately at Saint Germains , which I take the liberty to mention that your Lordp may endeavour all you can to get light into what they are doing at Saint Germains . By the last post from France wee found at the post house a letter from one Lebrun at Paris to Dunster at the three Lyons in Bedford Court , with an enclosed for Mr. Gray ; but upon reading it could find nothing therein but private concerns , and so sealed again and delivered. Your Lordp may please to be informed of your correspondent who this Gray is . Wee shall now expect the King with the first fair wind; for wee conclude his Majesty would be ready to embarke to morrow or Saturday. … Whitehall, 16 October 1699 I received by the post yesterday the favor of your Lordp’s letter of the 11/21 instant, and as soon as I understood the contents of it, and that Mills [ 1276 = have not , sic; a slip] was gone by the way of Rouen , I gott warrants prepared, and sent three severall messengers to watch his landing all along the coast [ 266 for 286 st ] where it may be thought he may land ; and at London too he is watched where he lives ; and besides wee still keep a messen[ge]r at Dover to watch him and Lord Drummond’s priest [enciphered pre-su-t ] these, for I think nothing would be more usefull then to take them and their letters . I have given directions likewise concerning Fowles , and will endeavor to have him met with . Tho I must acquaint your Lordp that there is no goldsmith [ 20 , c , for the s ] lives in Round Court , nor any body named Cockburne ; but there is one of that name, a thread man in Bedford Court , whom I have ordered enquiry to be made. I suppose your Lordp has heard of Clance the periwig maker ; he is gone lately to France . Your Lordp will please to have him observed and to give notice of his return . Wee are now looking out very impatiently for an Easterly wind to bring the King over. … The five slips are errors in Yard’s encoding: 1276 have not after Mills , where the sense wants nothing; 266 , an unassigned slot, for 286 st in coast ; pre-su-t for priest ; 20 ( c ) for an s in goldsmith ; and messen[ge]r , a syllable left out. The raw group-by-group decode, with the syllable joins, is in targets/yard1699/oct12_decoded.txt and oct16_decoded.txt .

Both letters answer letters from Manchester (of 7/17 and 11/21 October, the double dates being English Old Style and French New Style) and both are about watching people who cross between France and England. On the 12th messengers were already waiting at Dover for a man named Mills; on the 16th, having learned from Manchester’s letter that Mills had gone by the way of Rouen , Yard had warrants made out and three more messengers watching the coast where he might land, and his lodging in London watched as well. The Dover messenger was also to watch for Lord Drummond’s priest , and Yard wanted them and their letters taken. Enquiries after a Fowles, a Cockburne said to be a goldsmith in Round Court (there was none; there was a threadman of that name in Bedford Court) and a periwig maker called Clance, gone to France, follow the same pattern: names apparently sent from Paris, checked in London, and movements to be reported back. The larger news is in the 12 October letter. The Lords Justices of Ireland reported that many disaffected persons return dayly into that Kingdom and that there was some ill design against the Government ; similar reports came from the north about Scotland and about England; and all is said to be carryed on very privately at Saint Germains , the court of the exiled James II outside Paris. Yard asks Manchester to find out what they are doing there. The same letter shows the post office at work: a letter from one Lebrun in Paris to Dunster at the Three Lions in Bedford Court, with an enclosure for a Mr Gray, was taken out of the French post, read, found to hold nothing therein but private concerns , sealed again and delivered, and Manchester is asked who Gray is. The clear passages expect the King, William III, from Holland with the first fair wind. The Beinecke summaries of the neighbouring letters speak of “Mills and Lord Drummond’s priest” and “persons expected at Dover”, so the names decoded here agree with what the deciphered siblings say.

Three slots of the Yale sheet are hidden in a fold and illegible (1584, 1744, 1904, the third F-row entry of columns 10–12). None of them occurs in these two letters, but a letter that uses them would need a better image of the fold or the original. Yard’s own copy of the key differed from Manchester’s in at least the letter column and in 483. Three differences show in these letters; others may exist where the letters use a slot only once and the context carries the value. The unassigned slots are treated as nulls because the note calls the unnumbered ranges blanks and the 5 October decipherer skips four of them; that the numbered-but-empty slots are blanks too is an inference from their use, not stated on the sheet. Cole’s Memoirs of Affairs of State (1733) prints letters from Manchester’s embassy. It was not re-checked for these two letters, so a text of them in print, deciphered at the time, cannot yet be ruled out. Mills, Lebrun, Dunster, Gray, Fowles, Cockburne, Clance and Lord Drummond’s priest are not identified here.

The coded correspondence of the Orangist emigré d’Yvoy in London and Emmerich with the exiled Hereditary Prince (KHA A35-1450–1453): Dutch code numbers among clear French, deciphered at the time between the lines. Both code tables, London 1797–98 and 1799, are rebuilt from 371 glossed runs and tested page by page (78% and 81% against 26–27%). Daniel Bourdeau · posted 26 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letters Despatches of Maximiliaan Louis d’Yvoy from London and Hampton Court (1797–98) and from Emmerich and Münster (1799) to the Hereditary Prince Willem Frederik (later King Willem I), and the Prince’s numbered letters to d’Yvoy from Berlin and Schönhausen. Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A35 Willem I, inv. A35-1450 (1797), -1451 (1798), -1452 and -1453 (1799): 1,029 scans on the Koninklijke Verzamelingen site, 196 pages with code numbers. Not on DECODE. The cipher A Dutch word code: numbers of one to four digits for words, names and places, and syllable numbers for spelling names (15 505 512 = Tollius). The 1797–98 London table and the 1799 table are different: 1137 is Vrankryk in one and Holland in the other. How it was read Nearly every run carries a decipherment written over it at the time. 371 runs were transcribed, 322 of them glossed, and voted into two tables, 105 and 50 numbers; tested page by page, 78% and 81% of decoded words stand in the run’s own decipherment, against 26–27% in another run’s. What it says Orangist politics in exile: Tollius’s conferences, the Prince’s position, Prussia, Austria and Russia, the garrisons of Holland and Zeeland in 1799. The runs left undeciphered are a stock phrase, “hier achter is wat geschreven”: something is written on the back, in invisible ink. Still open Nothing in the code runs. The syllable numbers of both tables are thin, and the sympathetic-ink texts the pointer phrase announces are not on the scans. The Prince’s No. 22 to d’Yvoy, 22 September 1797: “het onderhoud met H.K.H.” over 122 625 202 703 1158, “Tollius” over 1154 15 505 512, and the run “voldaan van zyne eerste conferentien met Hunne Hoogh.” Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A35-1450, scan 221 (image 147106), via Koninklijke Verzamelingen.

Maximiliaan Louis van Hangest, baron d’Yvoy van Mijdrecht, was one of the Orangist emigrés who kept the Hereditary Prince informed after the flight of 1795. His letters to the Prince fill A35-1448 to 1458 in the Koninklijk Huisarchief; the four scanned volumes cover 1797 (317 scans), 1798 (175) and 1799 (220 and 317). They are written in French, with the sensitive words in numbers. The Prince’s own letters to d’Yvoy, numbered (No. 15, 16, 20–26 in 1797; 11–13 in 1798), are filed among them, usually three times over: a mounted original, a faint tissue copy and a photocopy. The KHA survey of 25 October flagged 28 pages from thumbnails. A second pass through all 1,029 scans found 196 pages with code numbers ( more_pages.tsv ). The 1799 letters are the heaviest, with 14 to 25 lines of numbers a page; the code nearly stops after August 1799.

Each run of numbers stands for Dutch words; the decipherment above it is Dutch even where the letter around it is French. Whole words and names have their own numbers; names not in the list are spelled with syllable numbers. The two tables share the form but not the values. London, 1797–98 (table L, 105 numbers) 1799 (table E, 50 numbers) 46 de, 85 en, 106 dat, 1073 van, 683 men, 1055 te, 1081 zal, 703 met, 111 ik, 684 niet 95 en, 161 in, 723 men, 743 met, 1083 van, 1271 zal, 1511 zyn 1107 Engeland, 1117 Pruissen, 1137 Vrankryk, 1167 Rusland, 1127 Oostenryk, 661 Keizer, 631 Koning 1137 Holland, 1157 Engeland, 1341 582 Zeeland, 1366 Nymegen, 1236 ’s Bosch 1056 Berlyn, 1156 Hamptoncourt, 1226 Parys, 1124 Pitt, 1488 Malmesbury, 1283 Vreede 1038 Erfprins, 1085 1071 Tuyll, 1068 Hertog, 33 508 544 de Garnizoenen Many runs end with a short stock phrase in d’Yvoy’s despatches: “hier 229 is wat”, “hier 229 is 43 609”, “op … drie is wat”. Where it is glossed (147205, 147226, 147351, 147412) it reads “hier achter is (wat) geschreven”: there is writing on the back. It announces a passage in sympathetic ink, the method the Orange family used in these years (the same practice runs through the Prince’s letters to his mother, targets/wilhelmina1795/ ).

Peut-être qu’à la réception {van dat antwoord} il pourra s’effectuer {een verandering in myne positie}. “… particularly the instructions you gave me in the first, concerning the conversation with His Royal Highness about the … instruction ; on which it seems to me you expressed very well all that could be said with modesty and emphasis . From letters of Tollius I learn that he is more or less satisfied with his first conferences with Their Highnesses, and I hope with him that the following ones will bring the good one may hope for … I have been promised a further answer to my letters sent over by Kiehl , so that until I have it I cannot act , as is known at Hampton Court . Perhaps on receipt of that answer a change in my position may come about.” The rest of the letter, in clear, asks what effect “la catastrophe arrivée à Paris” (18 Fructidor) will have on the negotiations of Lille and Udine.

Transcription. Agents transcribed every page with code numbers from the KHA images at full size, run by run: the clear words before and after, the numbers, the decipherment written over them, and a word-by-word alignment where the decipherment is placed over the numbers ( runs_a.txt to runs_e.txt ). Tables. tables.py votes each number’s value over all aligned runs, one table per code (the 1799 volume A35-1452–1453 against the rest). For the test each page is left out in turn: its numbers are decoded with the table built from the other pages, and a decoded word counts if it stands in the run’s own decipherment. Table L: 966 of 1,242 words (78%) against 321 (26%) in an unrelated run; table E: 130 of 161 (81%) against 43 (27%). Undeciphered runs. decode.py ran the 49 runs with no decipherment through both tables. Nearly all are the pointer phrase; its glossed instances fix 229 = achter and 43 609 / 43 669 = geschreven. Print. Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken II and III were searched in full text (Huygens retroboeken): d’Yvoy’s letters of 1795–96 and of 1799 (Nos. 676, 681, 686, 691, 705, 742, 750, 751, 781, 811) are printed; none of 1797–98, and not No. 22.

Septbr. 1797 Translation reading_no22_en.md # No. 22, the Hereditary Prince to d'Yvoy, Schönhausen, 22 September 1797: English translation Sir, Yesterday I received the two letters you were kind enough to write me on the 5th and 8th of this month, your Nos. 47 and 48; I hasten by this one to thank you for their contents, and above all for the instructions you were good enough to give me in the first, concerning *the conversation with His Royal Highness* about *the [...] instruction*; on which occasion it seems to me that you *expressed very well all that* could be *said with modesty and emphasis*. From letters of *Tollius* I learn that he is more or less *satisfied with his first conferences with Their Highnesses, and I hope with him that the following ones* will bring about the good one may hope from them, for the present [...] for the future. I have been promised *a further answer to* my *letters sent over by Kiehl*, so that until *I have received it I cannot act*, as is not unknown *at Hampton Court*. Perhaps on receipt *of that answer* *a change in my position* may come about. It is not yet known what influence the catastrophe in Paris [the coup of 18 Fructidor, 4 Sept 1797] has had or will have on the negotiations at Lille and Udine, but it still seems it cannot be wholly indifferent to them. Meanwhile every observer must be astonished that the scene, after being played so badly, brings no more confusion in Paris (for the gazettes tell us all is quiet and calm), and that those who have the upper hand use it with no more violence against the fallen party. We shall have to wait patiently for the end of this unhappy event before we can judge it properly. I am, with the most perfect consideration, Sir, your very humble and obedient servant.
